Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f:M\to N$ be smooth. Then there exist an open ball
$$ B\subseteq\mathbb R^m $$
containing $0$ and a smooth family of maps
$$ \mathcal F:M\times B\to N $$
such that $\mathcal F_0=f$ and, for every $p\in M$, the parameter map
$$ \mathcal F_p:B\to N,\qquad a\longmapsto \mathcal F(p,a), $$
is a submersion. In particular, the evaluation map $\mathcal F$ is a
submersion, so it is transverse to every closed embedded submanifold
$Z\subseteq N$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $Z\subseteq N$ be an embedded submanifold.
Then $F$ is **transverse to $Z$**, written $F\pitchfork Z$, when for every
$p\in F^{-1}(Z)$,

$$dF_p(T_pM)+T_{F(p)}Z=T_{F(p)}N.$$

If $F(M)\cap Z=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous, so $F\pitchfork Z$
still holds.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.
Under countable choice, every smooth manifold, also with boundary, admits a Riemannian metric.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Such a function is obtained by composing the collar coordinate with a smooth one-variable cutoff and extending by $1$. Put $\tau=\gamma^2$. Then $d\tau=0$ wherever $\tau=0$, and the zero set of $\tau$ lies inside $U$.

Where $\tau=0$, $d\tau=0$, so $G(p,a)=i(p)$ and its source derivative is $di_p$; [F5] and step 1.1 make it transverse to $S$. Since $\tau=0$ on a boundary collar, setting $G=i$ on $\partial F$ extends $G$ smoothly to $F\times B$, fixed near the boundary. Thus the total family is transverse to $S$.

Apply [F2] to $G|_{F^\circ\times B}$. Its good parameters are dense, because the bad set is null and every open parameter ball has positive measure. For each good parameter $a$, $G_a$ is transverse on $F^\circ$; near $\partial F$ it equals $i$, which is transverse by step 1.1. Hence $G_a$ is transverse on all of $F$.

Choose compatible Riemannian metrics on $F$ and $M$ using [F6]. At each $x\in F$, choose coordinate charts and a linear projection $P_x$ to a two-dimensional tangent plane so that $D(P_x\circ i)$ at $x$ is invertible. By [F5], shrink to a convex coordinate neighbourhood $U_x$ on which this derivative stays within one quarter of the least singular value of its value at $x$. Every sufficiently $C^1$-close map $j$ then has $P_x\circ j$ injective on $U_x$: integrate its derivative along the coordinate segment between two points to obtain a lower bound of one half that least singular value times their coordinate distance. Compactness gives a finite cover by such $U_x$ and a Lebesgue number $\delta>0$. For pairs at source distance at least $\delta$, compactness and injectivity of $i$ give a positive minimum target distance, which persists under sufficiently small $C^0$ perturbations. The differential of $i$ has a positive minimum norm on the compact unit tangent bundle, so immersion also persists under sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbations. Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

derivations.claim: A change of knot representative already comes with an oriented ambient isotopy by [F1]. Applying that isotopy to its ball-arc data carries the cut complement and its boundary collars to the new data, so the standard gluing produces an ambient-isotopic sum. A change of radius in one local straightening chart is the isotopy that rescales the standard ball radially while preserving its oriented diameter. This is an isotopy of compact ball-arc embeddings, so [A1] and [F3] extend it to an ambient isotopy of the knot sphere.

For two local oriented ball-arc charts centered at the same point, express them in one smooth coordinate chart. Their transition germ fixes the center, carries the positive tangent line of the knot to itself, and has positive determinant. Shrink to a common ball and use the smooth rescaling homotopy $G_s(x)=s^{-1}(G(sx)-G(0))$ for $s>0$, with $G_0(x)=DG_0(x)$. Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension at $s=0$. On a sufficiently small common ball the differentials stay uniformly close to the injective linear map $DG_0$, so every $G_s$ is an embedding and preserves the oriented diameter. The subgroup of invertible linear maps preserving that oriented line and the ambient orientation is path-connected: in line-normal coordinates its diagonal blocks lie in $(0,\infty)$ and $GL^+(2,\mathbb R)$, and the shear block contracts linearly to zero. Thus the chart germ is isotopic through oriented ball-arc embeddings to the fixed standard chart.

If the marked points differ, move the parameter point along the knot circle by a smooth isotopy of that circle. The resulting family of knot embeddings carries the short oriented subarc along a finite chain of local straightening charts; compactness of the parameter interval gives a common sufficiently small ball radius. Apply [F3] to this isotopy and to the chart isotopies of steps 1.1 and 1.2. The resulting ambient isotopies identify the cut complements with their boundary collars and preserve the fixed endpoint pairing in the standard gluing. Hence they induce an oriented ambient isotopy between the two connected-sum outputs.

derivations.claim: For commutativity, choose the symmetric standard two-ball model in [F1]. The orientation-preserving half-turn exchanging its two lobes carries each oriented knot tangle to the corresponding tangle in the swapped model and carries the fixed joining map to itself. It therefore gives an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy between the model outputs for $K\#J$ and $J\#K$; [F2] transfers this equality to arbitrary connected-sum data.

For associativity, place representatives of $K,J,L$ in three disjoint standard ball-arc pieces in a row and join consecutive pieces by the same fixed gluing. The constructions $(K\#J)\#L$ and $K\#(J\#L)$ then use the same three pieces and the same two joining maps; only the order in which the two gluings are performed differs. Since the gluings have disjoint boundary spheres, their order does not change the resulting oriented manifold or knot. By [F2], this common model represents both bracketings for arbitrary data.

For the identity, choose the standard unknot summand with a small ball meeting it in a trivial arc. Its spanning disk shows that the complementary arc is boundary-parallel and hence trivial. The connected-sum gluing replaces a short trivial arc of $K$ by another standard trivial arc. The ball-arc isotopy of [F2] identifies the output with $K$. Reversing the order gives the same argument for the left identity.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] and carry the knot through the same ambient isotopy. We now have the two standard hemispherical balls, each containing one proper arc of the knot. Cap each arc by a simple boundary arc, pushed slightly into a boundary collar; orient the cap to close the oriented original arc. Boundary caps give the same capped knot class: two simple arcs in a two-sphere joining the same two points are isotopic keeping the endpoints, with no other marked points to avoid. One explicit reduction puts the arcs transverse, removes an outermost bigon successively, and then slides the resulting disjoint arcs across the disk they cobound; all moves take place in surface disks and extend to their ball collars.

A small collar neighbourhood of each cap arc is a ball meeting the capped knot in one trivial arc. Delete these two ball-arc neighbourhoods. The remaining arcs are precisely the original two knot pieces, with endpoint collars on the common equator. Gluing by the fixed orientation-matching two-ball convention recovers $K$; the simultaneous boundary parametrization in [F1] makes the two sides agree. Straighten the cap collar and its positive local frame before gluing, which is a change of the local data allowed by [F2]. Hence this is the connected sum $K_1\#K_2$ in the stated convention. Let $D$ be a disk in one region of the complement of $\mathcal S$, with interior disjoint from that system and boundary a circle $c$ on a single sphere $A\in\mathcal S$. The circle misses the marks. Surgery on $A$ replaces it by the two spheres obtained by attaching parallel copies of $D$ to the two disks of $A\setminus c$, rounded and slightly pushed apart. The three spheres bound a standard sphere with three holes: take a product collar of $A$ and attach the thickened disk. Consequently the region on the other side of $A$ is unchanged after capping, except for extra punctures; all actual changes of capped knot occur in the one region containing the interior of $D$. Its other cap balls and arcs are untouched. This gives a precise local model in which the following cases are checked.

If $D$ has no mark, parity forces $c$ to leave both marks of $A$ in one disk of $A\setminus c$. Indeed otherwise one of the surgery spheres would meet the closed knot once, whereas a separating sphere has an even number of transverse intersections with a closed curve. Thus one surgery sphere is unmarked and the other has two marks. After capping the affected region, the unmarked sphere misses its closed knot. By [F2] its ball side not containing that connected knot is an empty ball. Filling or removing this empty ball and the adjoining product collars changes no capped knot. Discard the unmarked sphere and retain the twice-marked sphere. Hence this replacement preserves every nontrivial factor. The same argument covers empty ball and nested ball positions: it uses the side avoiding the capped knot, rather than a prespecified inside side.

If $D$ has one mark, parity instead forces each disk of $A\setminus c$ to have one mark. Both surgery spheres then have two marks. Let $C$ be the cap ball attached to $A$ on the affected region. Construct a proper disk $E\subset C$ with $\partial E=c$ by pushing one of the disks of $A\setminus c$ into the cap collar, fixing its boundary and rounding there. This disk is boundary parallel. Choose a simple boundary arc joining the two marks and crossing $c$ exactly once; a thin rectangular strip about that arc gives a boundary-parallel cap arc $\beta$ in $C$ meeting $E$ transversely exactly once. Explicitly the strip passes from the side of $E$ next to the first marked boundary disk to the side next to the other one, with a single normal crossing; away from that crossing it stays in disjoint boundary collars. Thus $\beta$ is trivial, and changing the original cap to $\beta$ is allowed by [F1]. Now $D\cup E$, rounded at $c$, meets the capped knot exactly twice: once on $D$ and once on $\beta$. It is the required marked decomposing sphere in the capped affected region. By [F1] the old factor $P$ is the sum $P'\#P''$ of the two new capped factors, with orientations inherited from the original knot. Since $P$ is prime, exactly one is the unknot and the other is $P$, by [F3]. Retain both new spheres temporarily and then delete the sphere separating that trivial region from its other neighbour. Deletion merges the neighbour with an unknot, so leaves its oriented knot class unchanged by [F3]. The net result is again a prime system with exactly the same unordered prime factors. The disk $E$ and the cap change lie entirely in $C$, disjoint from every other cap ball of the affected region. On the opposite region the three-holed-sphere collar of step 1.1 replaces only the cap at $A$: the short pieces of that cap become the caps on the two new spherical boundaries with the same endpoint pairing and orientation. Its other cap balls and their arcs stay pointwise fixed outside this collar. Therefore, even when that neighbour has several boundary spheres, deleting the sphere next to the trivial new region changes its capped knot precisely by oriented connected sum with the unknot, without changing any other attachment or factor.

To compare intersecting systems, choose a sphere of $\mathcal T$ that meets $\mathcal S$ and an innermost intersection disk on it containing at most one mark. Such a disk always exists: if there is one intersection circle, its two complementary disks have at most two marks in total, so choose a side with at most one. If there are several circles, the circle nesting tree has at least two leaf disks with disjoint interiors; since there are only two marks, one leaf contains at most one. Its interior misses $\mathcal S$. Use this disk in step 2.1 or step 2.2. The surgery copies can be pushed off $\mathcal T$ in its product neighbourhood and rounded near $c$; they introduce no new intersection circles, while $c$ disappears. Deleting a redundant sphere only decreases the count further. Thus the finite total number of intersection circles strictly decreases. Iterating makes the first system disjoint from $\mathcal T$, preserving its prime factor list throughout.

For completeness, the disjoint-system comparison is the same local calculation without surgery. Add the spheres of $\mathcal T$ one at a time to the disjoint first system, initially allowing trivial capped regions. In the capped region containing such a new sphere, its two marks give a connected-sum decomposition by [F1]. If the region's factor is prime, one new factor is that prime and the other the unknot; if it is the unknot, both new factors have genus zero by [F5] and hence are unknotted. Thus adding disjoint spheres preserves precisely the multiset of nontrivial prime factors. The union system therefore gives both original lists, which agree. A maximal factor ball replacement across a disjoint sphere consists of adding that sphere and deleting the old one; the same comparison proves its asserted preservation, including nested positions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Assume full AC. Put $B^j=[-1,1]^j$. Let $k+n=3$, $0\le k\le3$, and let $h:B^k\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^3$ be a topological embedding which is PL on a neighborhood of $\partial B^k\times\mathbb R^n$. There is an isotopy of embeddings $h_t$, $0\le t\le1$, starting at $h$, such that $h_1$ is PL on a neighborhood of $B^k\times B^n$, and
$$h_t=h\quad\text{on}\quad(\partial B^k\times\mathbb R^n)\cup\bigl(B^k\times(\mathbb R^n\setminus\operatorname{Int}(2B^n))\bigr).$$
For $n=0$ this means a boundary-relative straightening of the whole three-ball. More precisely $h_t=hP_t$ for an ambient TOP isotopy of the source with jointly continuous inverses and the displayed fixed set. No smooth isotopy is asserted.

This is a full-AC-qualified TOP-to-PL handle statement, including handles whose interior was only topologically parametrized. It does not by itself provide a finite triangulation of an arbitrary compact TOP manifold or discharge an original choice-free consumer.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Conversely, use [F1] to let a smooth embedding $e:D^2\to S^3$ parametrize a genus-zero spanning surface with oriented boundary $K$. Choose a point outside this spanning disk and the fixed standard disk; their union has empty interior, since finitely many surface slice charts cover each compact disk. Indeed Taylor's formula gives the smooth extension and, on a small disk, the derivatives are uniformly close to the injective linear map $r\,dE_0$; projection onto its image plane gives a uniform injectivity estimate by integration along line segments. Their images lie in the chart after decreasing $r$.

The final linear ellipse is isotopic to an oriented round circle in its plane: use the positive square root of its two-dimensional Gram matrix to deform its ordered independent spanning vectors to an orthonormal pair. Complete that pair by its positive normal to a positive ambient frame. Apply the same shrinking and linearization to the fixed standard disk in the common stereographic chart, obtaining an oriented round circle about its interior point $q$. Join the two round circles explicitly in this $\mathbb R^3$: move the center along the segment from $p$ to $q$, interpolate their positive radii, and rotate the first positive frame to the second through rotations in $SO(3)$ (successive rotations about coordinate axes suffice). Each intermediate circle is embedded, and the whole finite track is compact in the chart. A half-turn about a diameter reverses a circle orientation if required while preserving the ambient orientation. Reverse the standard disk shrinking to finish at the fixed standard unknot. Extend the concatenated circle isotopies by [F2]; each ambient diffeomorphism preserves orientation since it starts at the identity. Thus $K$ is the standard oriented unknot.

Since the intersection circles are disjoint and the arc $\alpha$ is connected and misses them, finite nesting gives a disk side of some circle containing neither $\alpha$ nor another intersection component. By [F4] this is an embedded disk $D\subset S$, disjoint from $K$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose two boundary components, with their induced orientations, have linking number $+1$. Let $F$ be the genus-one Seifert surface obtained by plumbing two positive Hopf bands in a square, with oriented core curves $a,b$ forming a positive handle basis, and choose the plumbing side so that $a^+$ bounds a disk in $S^3$ disjoint from $b$. The oriented boundary of this standard positive two-band plumbing is the right-handed trefoil. In the positive-push convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ with ordered basis $(a,b)$, the Seifert matrix is
$$
V=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Assume full AC. Use the canonical geometric Artin half twist in the oriented chart $(x,y,t)$, the canonical crossing sign $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, and the Seifert convention $\theta(u,v)=\operatorname{lk}(u^+,v)$. Let $F$ be the oriented braid Seifert surface consisting of two Seifert disks and the three crossing bands of the closure of $\sigma_1^3$. Label the bands in braid order $e_1,e_2,e_3$, oriented as edges from the first disk to the second. The cycle classes $a=e_1-e_2$ and $b=e_2-e_3$ form an integral basis. Order these two classes as $(u,v)$ so that $u\cdot_Fv=1$. Then
$$V_{(u,v)}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V+V^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.$$
In particular the signature is $-2$. The three pair-of-band annuli have core self-pairing $-1$, so they are positive Hopf bands when positive refers to the positively linked oriented boundary, rather than to core self-pairing $+1$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$, with $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ and use the positive normal convention $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K$ be the first homology of the infinite cyclic cover of $S^3\setminus K$ classified by total linking, with $t$ acting by the positive-meridian deck transformation. Let $\Delta_K(t)$ be the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal $E_0(A_K)$ in $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and write $p\doteq q$ when $p$ and $q$ differ by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\Lambda$. Then for every such $F$ and basis,

$$\det(V-tV^T)\doteq\Delta_K(t).$$

The determinant is $1$ for the empty $0\times0$ matrix when $g=0$. This formula concerns the polynomial $\Delta_K$; the existing knot-normalized fraction $D_K=\Delta_K/(1-t)$ is a separate invariant.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $K,J\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots, and let $K\#J$ be their oriented connected sum for a connected-sum datum using the fixed gluing convention. Then

$$\Delta_{K\#J}(t)\doteq \Delta_K(t)\Delta_J(t),$$

where each $\Delta$ is the generator of the zeroth elementary ideal of the one-variable Alexander module and $\doteq$ means equality up to multiplication by a unit $\pm t^k$ of $\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$. The statement is independent of the local connected-sum choices and of the Seifert surfaces and bases used to compute the polynomials.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented surface with oriented boundary $K$, let $V$ be the matrix of the Seifert pairing $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ in an ordered integral basis, and let $\omega\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$. Define the **Levine–Tristram Hermitian matrix** by
$$H_\omega(V)=(1-\omega)V+(1-\bar\omega)V^T.$$
It is Hermitian because $V$ is real and $\bar\omega=\omega^{-1}$. Its signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues, both counted with multiplicity and with zero eigenvalues omitted. When $\Delta_K(\omega)\ne0$, define $\sigma_\omega(K)$ to be this signature. At a root $\omega_0\ne1$ of $\Delta_K$, define $\sigma_{\omega_0}(K)$ to be the arithmetic mean of the two one-sided limits of $\sigma_{e^{i\theta}}(K)$ as $\theta$ approaches an argument of $\omega_0$ from below and above. The invariance and one-sided-existence lemmas justify treating these values as independent of the chosen surface and basis.

Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

By [F1] and [F2],
$$\Delta_T(t)\doteq\det(V-tV^T)=\det\begin{pmatrix}t-1&t\\-1&t-1\end{pmatrix}=(t-1)^2+t=t^2-t+1.$$
For $-T^*$ use the reflected spanning surface with its surface orientation reversed, so its boundary is the reversed reflected knot. Its positive normal is the reflected original positive normal: ambient reflection and surface reversal each negate the orientation, so their effects cancel in the normal-first convention. Reflection negates linking. The transported homology basis on this actual surface consequently has matrix $-V$. Its determinant is $\det(-V+tV^T)=\det(V-tV^T)$, since the matrix size is two. The two determinants evaluate to $3$ at $t=-1$, so this parameter is nonroot and [F3] applies directly, with no root-average ambiguity.

By [F2], the actual boundary connected-sum surfaces of $G=T\#T$ and $Q=T\#(-T^*)$ have matrices $V\oplus V$ and $V\oplus(-V)$. Their block determinants both equal $(t^2-t+1)^2$, proving the two Alexander-polynomial identities up to units. Also
$$H_{-1}(V)=2(V+V^T)=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-2\\-2&-4\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its eigenvalues on the vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are $-6$ and $-2$, respectively. Thus $\sigma_{-1}(T)=-2$ and $\sigma_{-1}(-T^*)=2$. The corresponding block forms give $\sigma_{-1}(G)=-4$ and $\sigma_{-1}(Q)=-2+2=0$. These are actual knot-invariant values by [F3], since the sum polynomials at $-1$ equal $9\ne0$. In particular $|\sigma_{-1}(G)|=4$ as stated.

By [F4], $T$ and $T^*$ are nontrivial prime oriented knots. Reversal of knot orientation also preserves these properties: reverse both factors and the two local oriented arcs in any purported nontrivial connected-sum presentation of $-T^*$ to obtain a nontrivial presentation of $T^*$; reversing again is the inverse operation, and the unknot remains the unknot. Thus $-T^*$ is prime. The signatures in step2.1 show that $T$ and $-T^*$ are distinct oriented knot types, since an oriented ambient isotopy would preserve [F3]'s signature. Therefore the displayed two-prime decompositions have respective multisets $\{T,T\}$ and $\{T,-T^*\}$, which are different. By [F4]'s actual oriented Schubert uniqueness they are the prime-factor multisets of $G$ and $Q$, independent of a chosen decomposition. 1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On a compact height band without critical points, the restriction of height to the surface has a smooth field $X$ with $dz(X)=1$: in any surface chart divide a coordinate field by its nonzero height derivative, and combine finitely many such fields by a smooth partition near the compact band. Its flow carries the level circles through the band. Existence for the entire height interval follows by covering the compact band by finitely many flow charts, choosing a common positive short time, and restarting; the trajectory remains in the band until its height reaches an endpoint. Projecting each moving circle to its horizontal plane gives a smooth isotopy of disjoint plane curves. Its velocity has a smooth planar extension near the circles by their normal collar charts; finitely many cutoffs give a compactly supported extension. Its planar flow therefore straightens these curves simultaneously, level by level. In ambient coordinates use $(x,z)\mapsto(g_z(x),z)$ for these plane diffeomorphisms, cutting it off beyond the end levels. Consequently every regular end of the piece can be made vertical. The construction can be made fixed near its attachment to a critical neighborhood.

Move the horizontal caps toward the critical level, stopping in a sufficiently thin slab about that level; in a regular collar this is exactly shortening a vertical cylinder and translating its cap. With nested caps perform the move on the innermost disk first and keep the stopping heights distinct in the order imposed by disjointness. This prevents intersections: outside the moving collar the only possible obstruction is another cap over a nested planar disk, and that cap has already been moved to a nearer stopping height or is kept beyond the moving one. Use positive, strictly monotone changes of the height coordinate along each cylinder, constant near its fixed end, to implement these moves; on the cap use the corresponding translation. Smooth corner rounding is done in disjoint collar neighborhoods. These are isotopies of the capped surface, and [F2] extends them ambiently. The same shortening applies in a component with no critical point, using any intermediate level.

At a saddle use the chart $z=z(p)+u^2-v^2$. Outside a small rectangle about the saddle the regular sheets can be made vertical by step 1.1. Viewed in the horizontal plane, the two circles on the two-component side are joined by the projected saddle rectangle; its interior misses those circles. There are exactly two possibilities: their bounded disks are disjoint, or one disk lies inside the other. To justify completeness, each circle bounds the unique disk in the plane by [F1]. The connected second circle avoids the first and hence lies entirely in its disk interior or its exterior; applying the same argument with the two interchanged gives precisely disjoint or nested disks. The rectangle lies in the region adjacent to both of its attaching arcs: outside both disks in the disjoint case and in the annulus between them in the nested case. A different region would force it to cross one of the two circles. The saddle's other level circle is the boundary obtained by the band reconnection. Reverse height if necessary so this is the one-component side.

With no critical point the connected uncapped piece is a cylinder: the flow in step 1.1 identifies it with one level circle times an interval. After shortening and straightening it is the vertical wall over a plane circle, with one disk cap at each end. Its bounded region is $D^2\times I$ in the disk coordinates from [F1]. This is a ball after rounding: replace the product corners in the disk-radius/height half-plane by circular arcs; the rounded solid is a smooth convex cylinder with rounded ends, radially parametrizable from its center. If there is a maximum or a minimum, the critical chart in [F2] is a paraboloid disk. The regular part is a cylinder attached to its boundary, by step 1.1. Shorten that cylinder into the chart. The paraboloid and its opposite planar cap bound a region $\{(u,v,t):0\le t\le c-u^2-v^2\}$, or its reflection. It is a ball, since rounding its edge gives a convex solid with a smooth radial parametrization; a radial rescaling is constant linear near the center and adjusted near the boundary. Thus these three cases give standard balls.

In the disjoint-disk case, straighten the two attaching arcs in the boundary collars of their planar disks. The projected union of the two disks and the connecting rectangle is a disk: shrink the disks in their parametrizations to end caps, straighten the rectangle in its product coordinates, and round to a stadium. All remaining interval parametrizations extend over their collars by increasing interpolation, so this is an actual disk parametrization. The capped saddle bounds the solid made from the two short disk cylinders by a single thickened rectangle joining one disk window of each. Indeed, away from the rectangle its boundary is exactly the two vertical walls and their horizontal caps; across the rectangle its boundary has the reconnection prescribed by $u^2-v^2$. Rounding the rectangle's two lower or upper edges produces that saddle chart, and rounding the other edges gives precisely the cap collars. The two cylinders are balls by step 3.1. The thickened rectangle is a ball meeting the first cylinder in one disk, and its union with that cylinder meets the second cylinder in one disk. Two applications of [F3] therefore make this solid a ball.

In the nested-disk case let $D_i\subset\operatorname{Int}D_o$ be the inner and outer disks. Their intervening closed annulus is a smooth annulus by the two marked-disk/annulus construction of numbered clauses 12.1–13.1 of [F1]'s smooth-input normal-form proof. The joining rectangle is a crosscut of this annulus. Cutting along its central joining arc leaves a connected surface: a path can be rerouted from one side of the cut to the other around either of the two boundary circles before their marked attaching intervals are removed. Its boundary is one circle and its Euler characteristic is $0+1=1$, since cutting the rectangle replaces one band by two boundary intervals. The finite surface normal form in [F1] therefore gives a topological disk, and its smooth-input construction gives a smooth disk. Equivalently the curve on the one-component side bounds the annulus slit along the joining rectangle. The bounded solid of the capped saddle is an outer short disk cylinder with an inner short disk cylinder indented into one end; the indent's boundary window is opened to the outer wall by the thickened joining rectangle. The indented cylinder together with that rectangle is a ball meeting the outer cylinder's boundary in one disk: this window is the union of its inner disk window and the strip running to the outer boundary, rounded along their shared interval. This description is checked fiberwise away from the rectangle: a point of $D_o\setminus D_i$ has the full outer vertical interval and a point of $D_i$ has that interval shortened by the inner cap. Along the rectangle these intervals join at their endpoints in the single local reconnection $u^2-v^2$; rounding gives the prescribed saddle. The indented cylinder and joining rectangle are balls glued along one window, hence their union is a ball by [F3]. Removing this boundary-attached ball from the outer cylinder leaves a ball by [F3]. This proves the nested case.

A connected regular piece has one circle at each end; an extremum piece has one; and a saddle piece has the three boundary circles just analyzed. There are no additional ends in the connected component: the regular flow supplies cylinders and the single critical chart supplies respectively the disk or the single band. Thus steps 4.1–4.2 exhaust the capped components that are spheres. Every straightening used an embedding isotopy, so it carries the constructed ball back to a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the original capped sphere. For surgeries performed successively at finitely many regular levels, the innermost choice ensures that each cap interior misses the remaining surface, and sufficiently small distinct collar widths keep all new caps disjoint. Their components have exactly the form used in steps 1.1–2.1, so the final assertion follows as well.

derivations.claim: Choose a point of $S^3$ outside $S$ and use its stereographic chart to regard $S$ as a compact smoothly embedded sphere in $\mathbb R^3$. By [F1] choose a direction whose restricted height is Morse, and rotate it to the $z$ direction. Separate its finitely many critical values by the finite small perturbation in [F1]. Realize that perturbation geometrically by retaining the $x,y$ coordinates and changing only $z$. A sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation and its straight interpolation are embeddings: finitely many graph charts retain a nonzero rank-two minor and local injectivity, while pairs of source points outside those chart neighborhoods have a positive image-separation minimum by compactness. Choose the perturbation below both bounds. By [F5] this is an ambient isotopy of $S^3$, supported away from the stereographic point. It therefore suffices to prove that the resulting sphere, with excellent Morse height, bounds a smooth standard ball in $\mathbb R^3$.

Choose finitely many regular heights between consecutive critical values. A level meets the sphere in finitely many smooth disjoint circles: its preimage is a compact regular one-manifold, and finitely many connected local interval charts cover it. Each circle bounds a planar smooth disk by [F2]. Choose an innermost circle, so that this disk's interior misses every other level circle and hence misses the sphere. In a sufficiently thin regular band around the level remove the sphere's annular collar of that circle and replace it by the two horizontal disks at the band's ends. The level curves vary smoothly, so their disks at nearby heights remain disjoint from the rest of the surface after a sufficiently small band shrink. Round the two seams in that band. This is surgery on the sphere along a disk whose interior misses the surface.

Every such surgery replaces one smooth sphere by two smooth spheres. Indeed its circle splits that sphere into two disk regions by [F2], and each region, with the added cap, is a smooth sphere: the boundary gluing is a smooth circle map and extends over a disk by the angular interpolation used in [F2]'s normal-form construction. Now repeat step 1.2 on each remaining circle of that regular level, always innermost among the remaining circles and with a new sufficiently small collar width. Earlier horizontal caps are kept at distinct nearby levels, and the new width is chosen smaller than their positive distances from the chosen level. There are finitely many circles. Then repeat at the finitely many other chosen regular levels, with disjoint level neighborhoods. The outcome is a finite disjoint collection of smooth spheres, each made from a connected piece of the original sphere between successive cutting levels, together with horizontal caps. Each such piece contains at most one height critical point.

By [F3] each final sphere bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. We shall reverse the surgeries and prove inductively that each sphere then present bounds a smooth embedded standard ball. No assertion that all their chosen balls are disjoint is needed: balls bounded by disjoint spheres may be nested.

Consider the reverse of the last unreversed surgery, whose two output spheres bound balls $A$ and $B$ by the inductive assertion. In its product disk neighborhood the two added cap disks can be moved toward each other until both occupy the original surgery disk $D$; equivalently shrink the normal coordinate of the deleted annular collar to zero. Their remaining boundaries are disjoint. The move is an isotopy up to its endpoint on each individual ball, because the cap has a product collar and its boundary annulus is shortened monotonically; at the endpoint it merely meets the other ball's boundary in $D$. An arbitrarily small corner rounding reverses this motion and recovers the pre-surgery sphere. The balls now have either disjoint interiors and intersection exactly $D$, or one is contained in the other, with their boundaries meeting exactly in $D$. To check that these alternatives exhaust the possibilities, first take their disjoint cap positions. The complement of a known embedded ball in $\mathbb R^3$ is connected: [F4] carries that ball to a round one by a compactly supported ambient isotopy. Hence each connected sphere disjoint from the other's boundary lies wholly inside or wholly outside its ball. If neither ball contains the other's boundary, their interiors are disjoint; otherwise one ball is inside the other. The product cap motion preserves the corresponding alternative and makes their boundary contact exactly $D$.

In the disjoint-interior case the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\cup_D B$. This union is a ball by disk absorption [F4]. In the nested case, relabel so that $B\subset A$; the pre-surgery sphere is the rounded boundary of $A\setminus\operatorname{Int}B$, where $B$ meets $\partial A$ in the disk $D$. Disk removal [F4] says that this too is a ball. These boundary identifications can be checked in $D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$: the pre-surgery annular wall is the side $\partial D\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$, whereas surgery inserts the faces $D\times\{-\varepsilon,\varepsilon\}$; all surfaces agree outside that neighborhood. Thus the induction gives a smooth standard ball bounded by the original excellent-height sphere. Undoing the initial small ambient isotopy gives a smooth embedded standard ball bounded by the given $S$.

Apply [F4] to that parametrized embedded ball, using the stereographic chart, to carry it by an ambient isotopy to a small Euclidean round ball. Translation and positive dilation in $\mathbb R^3$ extend smoothly across its compactifying point: they are the usual stereographic conformal transformations of $S^3$, and their parameter paths give smooth ambient isotopies. They carry the round boundary sphere to the unit sphere, the standard equator in this stereographic convention. Concatenate with the preceding isotopies, using smooth stationary reparametrizations. This gives the claimed $H_t$, starting at the identity. The two components and both ball diffeomorphisms are now the inverse images of the two standard open hemispheres and their closures under $H_1$. The two restrictions agree on $S$ because they restrict one ambient diffeomorphism, and pulling back the standard equator's two-sided collar gives a common collar with the same property.

citations.quote: Let $P$ and $Q$ be compact piecewise-linear polyhedra. A **piecewise-linear map** $f:P\to Q$ is a map that is simplicial after suitable finite subdivisions of triangulations of $P$ and $Q$. A **subpolyhedron** $A$ of $Q$ is a subset represented by the realization of a subcomplex in some finite linear triangulation of $Q$. A map $f:P\to Q$ is a **piecewise-linear embedding** if it is piecewise-linear, its image $f(P)$ is a subpolyhedron of $Q$, and $f:P\to f(P)$ is a piecewise-linear homeomorphism. A finite simplicial triangulation of a closed piecewise-linear $n$-manifold is **combinatorial** if the link of every $k$-simplex is a piecewise-linear sphere of dimension $n-k-1$. Thus in a closed combinatorial $3$-manifold every triangular face has link $S^0$ and is incident to exactly two tetrahedra.

Two finite linear simplicial subdivisions $K_1,K_2$ of a fixed finite Euclidean simplicial complex have a common finite linear simplicial refinement. This asserts refinement of triangulations of the same embedded polyhedron, not of arbitrary abstractly homeomorphic triangulations.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex.

A **subcomplex** of $K$ is a subfamily $L \subseteq K$ that is itself closed
under taking subsets.

If $\sigma \in K$, its **closure** is the subcomplex
$$\overline{\sigma}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma\}.$$
More generally, if $A \subseteq K$, its closure is
$$\overline{A}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma \text{ for some } \sigma \in A\}.$$

For a simplex $\sigma \in K$, the **closed star** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{St}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \sigma \cup \tau \in K\},$$
and the **open star** is the union, after realization, of the relative
interiors of simplices $\rho\in K$ with $\sigma\subseteq\rho$.

The **link** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{Lk}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \tau \cap \sigma=\varnothing \text{ and } \sigma \cup \tau \in K\}.$$

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Continuity is as in [[def-continuous-map-top]],
injections, surjections and bijections as in
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]].

- $f$ is an **open map** if $f[U]$ is open in $Y$ for every open $U \subseteq X$.
- $f$ is a **closed map** if $f[F]$ is closed in $Y$ for every closed
  $F \subseteq X$.
- $f$ is a **homeomorphism** if $f$ is a continuous bijection whose inverse
  $f^{-1} : Y \to X$ is also continuous. The spaces are **homeomorphic**, written
  $X \cong Y$, when a homeomorphism $X \to Y$ exists.
- $f$ is an **embedding** if $f$ is injective and the corestriction
  $f_0 : X \to f[X]$, $f_0(x) = f(x)$, is a homeomorphism onto $f[X]$ carrying
  the subspace topology inherited from $Y$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**The inverse in the third clause exists because $f$ is a bijection**, and it is
the unique two-sided inverse ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); no choice
principle is involved. Continuity of $f^{-1}$ is a genuine additional demand: a
continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism, and this page records that
failure as a false statement with a two-point witness.

**Open, closed and homeomorphism are three different conditions.** A
homeomorphism is continuous by definition, but an open map need not be continuous
and a closed map need not be continuous; and continuity implies neither openness
nor closedness. An open map need
not be closed and a closed map need not be open, and Sierpinski space
$S = \{a,b\}$ with open point $b$ ([[def-standard-topologies]]) witnesses both
failures at once: the constant map $S \to S$ with value $b$ is open, since the
image of every nonempty set is the open set $\{b\}$, and is not closed, since the
image of the closed set $\{a\}$ is $\{b\}$, whose complement $\{a\}$ is not open;
the constant map with value $a$ is closed and not open by the same computation
read the other way. What is true
is that for a **continuous bijection** the three notions collapse: it is a
homeomorphism exactly when it is open, exactly when it is closed. That is proved
in the next item and is not assumed here.

**Topological properties.** A **property of topological spaces** is a condition
$P$ that is either true or false of each space. $P$ is a **topological property**
(one is also said to be *preserved by homeomorphism*, or *invariant*) when
$X \cong Y$ implies that $P(X)$ and $P(Y)$ have the same truth value. Since
$\cong$ is an equivalence relation on spaces — the identity is a homeomorphism,
inverses and composites of homeomorphisms are homeomorphisms, all three verified
in the next item — a topological property is exactly one that is constant on each
$\cong$-class.

**What a homeomorphism transports.** If $h : X \to Y$ is a homeomorphism then
$U \mapsto h[U]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{T}_X$ onto $\mathcal{T}_Y$, with
inverse $V \mapsto h^{-1}[V]$: both maps are well defined because $h$ and
$h^{-1}$ are continuous, and they are mutually inverse because $h$ is a
bijection. So a homeomorphism is an isomorphism of the structure "a set together
with a distinguished family of subsets", and every notion defined from the open
sets alone — closed, closure, interior, boundary, dense, convergence of
sequences, continuity of maps into and out of the space — is carried across by
it. Anything defined from extra data, such as a metric or an order, is not, and
that distinction is exactly what the phrase *topological property* is for.

Write $I=[0,1]$ with its usual subspace topology, as in [[def-path-connected]]. Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces, and let $f,g:X\to Y$ be continuous maps ([[def-continuous-map-top]]).

A **homotopy from $f$ to $g$** is a continuous map

$$H:X\times I\longrightarrow Y$$

from the product space ([[def-product-topology]]) such that $H(x,0)=f(x)$ and $H(x,1)=g(x)$ for every $x\in X$. When such an $H$ exists, $f$ and $g$ are **homotopic**, written $f\simeq g$.

Let $A\subseteq X$ carry the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). The homotopy $H$ is a **homotopy relative to $A$**, or a homotopy **rel $A$**, when

$$H(a,t)=f(a)=g(a)\qquad(a\in A,\ t\in I).$$

Thus a homotopy rel $A$ can exist only when $f|_A=g|_A$, and every ordinary homotopy is a homotopy rel $\varnothing$. We write $f\simeq_A g$ when a homotopy rel $A$ exists.

If $\alpha,\beta:I\to Y$ are paths with the same initial point and the same terminal point ([[def-path-connected]]), a **path homotopy from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ relative to the endpoints** is a homotopy $H:I\times I\to Y$ rel $\{0,1\}$. Explicitly,

$$H(s,0)=\alpha(s),\quad H(s,1)=\beta(s),\quad H(0,t)=\alpha(0)=\beta(0),\quad H(1,t)=\alpha(1)=\beta(1).$$

The first coordinate $s$ parametrises the path and the second coordinate $t$ parametrises the deformation.

derivations.claim: Choose $R>1$ so large that $K\cup f(K)$ lies in the open radius-$R$ ball; this is possible because the continuous image of a compact set is compact, and compact Euclidean sets are bounded. Set $L=R+1$. Define an increasing homeomorphism $\rho:[0,\infty)\to[0,L)$ by $\rho(r)=r$ for $r\le R$ and $\rho(r)=R+(r-R)/(1+r-R)$ for $r\ge R$. The radial map $y(0)=0$, $y(x)=\rho(\lVert x\rVert)x/\lVert x\rVert$ for $x\ne0$, is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R^n$ onto the open radius-$L$ ball, and it is the identity on the closed radius-$R$ ball. On the open radius-$L$ ball put $g=y\circ f\circ y^{-1}$. This is a homeomorphism there.

Extend $g$ by the identity on the radius-$L$ sphere. To verify continuity there, put $r=\lVert x\rVert$ and $s=\lVert f(x)\rVert$. The displacement bound gives $s\ge r-C$. For $r>C$, insert $f(x)/r$ between the two unit vectors to obtain
$$\left\lVert\frac{f(x)}{s}-\frac{x}{r}\right\rVert\le\frac{|s-r|}{r}+\frac{C}{r}\le\frac{2C}{r}.$$
Consequently
$$\lVert y(f(x))-y(x)\rVert\le |\rho(s)-\rho(r)|+\rho(r)\frac{2C}{r}\le (L-\rho(s))+(L-\rho(r))+\frac{2LC}{r}.$$
The right side tends to zero as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over directions, since $s\ge r-C$ and $\rho$ is increasing with limit $L$. For an interior point $z=y(x)$ approaching a boundary point $b$, the equality $\lVert z\rVert=\rho(r)$ forces $r\to\infty$, and $\lVert g(z)-b\rVert\le\lVert g(z)-z\rVert+\lVert z-b\rVert$ tends to zero by this bound. This proves continuity directly. The inverse $f^{-1}$ has the same displacement bound: if $z=f(x)$ then $\lVert f^{-1}(z)-z\rVert=\lVert x-f(x)\rVert\le C$. Applying the same calculation to $f^{-1}$ gives the continuous inverse extension. Extend once more by the identity outside the closed radius-$L$ ball to obtain a homeomorphism $G$ of $\mathbb R^n$. The formulas and their inverse formulas agree on the joining sphere.

The set $U=\{x:\lVert x\rVert<R,\ \lVert f(x)\rVert<R\}$ is an open neighborhood of $K$. On $U$ both $y^{-1}(x)=x$ and $y(f(x))=f(x)$, so $G(x)=f(x)$. Thus any piecewise linearity of $f$ on an open neighborhood of $K$ is retained after intersecting that neighborhood with $U$. This is an equality of actual local maps, rather than an approximation statement about their images.

For $0<t\le1$ define $G_t(x)=tG(x/t)$ when $\lVert x\rVert\le tL$, and $G_t(x)=x$ when $\lVert x\rVert\ge tL$; put $G_0(x)=x$. The branches agree at $\lVert x\rVert=tL$ because $G$ fixes the radius-$L$ sphere. Each $G_t$ is a homeomorphism, with inverse given by the same formula using $G^{-1}$; it fixes every point outside the radius-$tL$ ball. The formulas give joint continuity for $t>0$. At $t=0$, both $x$ and its image lie in the radius-$tL$ ball whenever a point moves, so $\lVert G_t(x)-x\rVert\le2tL$. This proves joint continuity at zero, uniformly in $x$. The identical estimate applies to the inverse family, hence $(x,t)\mapsto(G_t(x),t)$ is a homeomorphism with continuous inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(G_t^{-1}(x),t)$. Therefore $G_t$ is an ambient isotopy, supported in the radius-$L$ ball, from the identity to $G$. Together with step 2.1 this proves all conclusions.

Let $Q$ be a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron with a fixed finite linear triangulation $T$. If $f:P\to Q$ is a piecewise-linear embedding of a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron, then some finite subdivision $T'$ of $T$ contains $f(P)$ as the realization of a subcomplex.

derivations.claim: Attach an external collar and denote the resulting polyhedron by $Q^+=(Q\times\{1\})\cup(P\times[0,1])$, identifying $P\subset Q$ with $P\times\{1\}$. This is a polyhedron: triangulate the compact marked part of $Q$ with $P$ a subcomplex, triangulate its product prisms compatibly, and glue the equal marked faces. Outside this compact part keep the original locally finite triangulation. A local collar chart about $a\in P$, shrunk to the closed star $S_a=a*L_a$ of a vertex in a finite triangulation of $P$, identifies $S_a\times[1,2]$ with a neighborhood in $Q$ of that star. Combining it with the external collar gives $S_a\times[0,2]\subset Q^+$. The product is the cone from $(a,1)$ over $(L_a\times[0,2])\cup(S_a\times\{0,2\})$. Triangulate that boundary and cone it to $(a,1)$. Moving the cone vertex to $(a,1/2)$ and extending linearly on the cone simplices defines a piecewise linear homeomorphism of this product fixed on the displayed cone base, which is the relative frontier of the local neighborhood in $Q^+$. The remaining sides, if the star meets the boundary of $P$, may move along the boundary of $Q^+$. Both cone decompositions cover the product: on every radial line in the star factor the product has a single interval in each height direction, so each ray from either vertex has a unique final boundary point. Extend this map by the identity to $Q^+$ and call it $h_a$.

On the external collar, $h_a$ preserves the $P$ coordinate and decreases the height weakly. In a cone simplex this follows directly from affine coordinates: only the cone vertex changes, by the vertical displacement $-1/2$, so a point with cone-vertex coefficient $\lambda$ has the same first coordinate and height reduced by $\lambda/2$. The decrease is strict for points over the relative interior $S_a\setminus L_a$ with height strictly between $0$ and $2$. Compactness provides finitely many such star interiors covering $P$. Compose their pushes in any fixed order to obtain a piecewise linear homeomorphism $h'$ of $Q^+$. Every point $(x,1)$ is then sent to $(x,t(x))$ with $0<t(x)<1$: at least one selected star contains $x$ in its interior, that push strictly decreases the height, subsequent pushes cannot increase it, and all pushes fix height zero and are injective. Since each push preserves the ordered vertical intervals in the external collar, $h'(Q)\cap(P\times[0,1])$ is exactly the region $T=\{(x,s):t(x)\le s\le1\}$. Also $h'(Q)$ contains all of $Q\times\{1\}$, since the inverse of every push increases height on any point at height at least one in its local chart.

The function $t$ is piecewise linear on a finite subdivision of $P$: the graph $h'(P)$ is a finite polyhedron projecting bijectively to $P$, and subdividing the projection gives an affine bijection on every simplex with affine inverse on its image. Refine its projected cells compatibly using [F1]. For each simplex $A$ in this subdivision, $T\cap(A\times[0,1])$ is a convex prism cut out by the affine bottom $s=t(x)$ and the constant top $s=1$. Its faces correspond exactly to the faces of $A\times[0,1]$. Construct compatible piecewise linear homeomorphisms between these prisms by induction over their faces: prescribe the identity on the top, the projection $(x,t(x))\mapsto(x,0)$ on the bottom, use the already constructed face maps on the vertical sides, and cone from interior points to extend over each remaining cell. The finite convex cell triangulation argument in [F1] verifies bijectivity and a piecewise linear inverse. These maps paste to $g:T\to P\times[0,1]$, fixed on the top and sending the graph to the bottom by its first coordinate. Extend $g$ by the identity on $Q\times\{1\}$ to obtain a piecewise linear homeomorphism $h'(Q)\to Q^+$.

The composite $h=g\circ h'|_Q:Q\to Q^+$ is a piecewise linear homeomorphism and sends each $x\in P$ to $(x,0)$. Pull back the external collar by $h$: put $c(x,s)=h^{-1}(x,s)$. This is a piecewise linear embedding with the required bottom restriction, and its half-open image is an open neighborhood because $P\times[0,1)$ is an open neighborhood of $P\times\{0\}$ in $Q^+$. A piecewise linear boundary chart is a local product chart of the required kind, so the manifold assertion follows. Only the finite local cover and finite subdivisions were selected; no countable or arbitrary-index choice assumption is used.

For a finite Euclidean simplicial complex $K$ define its simplex mesh $m(K)$ to be the maximum diameter of its nonempty simplices, with the separate convention $m(K)=0$ if there are none. If $\dim K=n\geq1$, then
$$m(\operatorname{sd}^rK)\leq\left(\frac n{n+1}\right)^r m(K)\longrightarrow0.$$
Every nonempty vertex star has diameter at most $2m(K)$. Zero-dimensional and vertex-free complexes have mesh zero. The metric is the original Euclidean metric transported through barycentric realization, not a new unit-edge metric at each subdivision.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. derivations.claim: If $P$ is empty, take $V$ empty, with the empty triangulation and homotopy; all assertions hold. Otherwise subdivide $K$ sufficiently finely that the closed union of its simplices meeting $P$ lies in $W$. To see this, when $M\setminus W$ is nonempty its compactness and that of $P$ give a positive distance between them in the finite realization metric; take the mesh smaller than that distance. If $W=M$, there is no restriction. After one further barycentric subdivision, the subdivided $P$ is a full subcomplex: vertices of a simplex are a chain of faces of the preceding triangulation, so if all those vertices belong to the subdivided $P$, every face in the chain belongs to $P$, and the whole chain simplex belongs to it. Denote this final triangulation again by $K$. For each vertex $v$ put $a_v=1$ when $v\in P$ and $a_v=0$ otherwise, and extend linearly on simplices to a function $r:M\to[0,1]$. Fullness gives $r^{-1}(1)=P$. Set $V=\{r\ge1/2\}$. This is compact, contains the relatively open neighborhood $\{r>1/2\}$ of $P$, and lies in $W$: every simplex meeting $V$ has a vertex in $P$ and hence belongs to the closed union chosen above.

On a simplex with barycentric coordinates $(\lambda_v)$ and with $r\ge1/2$, define a homotopy by replacing each coordinate at a vertex of $P$ by $\lambda_v(r+t(1-r))/r$ and each other coordinate by $(1-t)\lambda_v$, for $0\le t\le1$. The new coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one; their sum at the vertices of $P$ is $r+t(1-r)\ge1/2$. The formulas agree on common faces and have denominator bounded below by $1/2$, so they give a continuous homotopy of $V$ into itself. At time zero it is the identity, at time one it maps into the face spanned by the $P$ vertices, which lies in $P$ by fullness, and it fixes every point of $P$ throughout. This is the required strong deformation retraction. It also gives a path in $V$ from each point to $P$, so $V$ is connected when $P$ is.

The cuts of each simplex by $r=1/2$ are convex polyhedral cells and agree on common faces. Their finite collection has a compatible triangulation by [F2], including their faces in $P$ and in $\partial M$. Thus $V$, its level frontier $L=\{r=1/2\}$, and its boundary trace $A=V\cap\partial M$ are finite subpolyhedra. It remains to verify the manifold and surface assertions, rather than inferring them merely from this triangulation.

Let $x\in L$, and let $\sigma$ be the unique simplex whose relative interior contains $x$. Since its barycentric coordinates are all positive and their weighted sum is $1/2$, $\sigma$ has both a vertex of $P$ and one outside $P$. Choose a vector $d$ in its affine span with coordinate sum zero and with $dr(d)=1$, for example the difference between such two vertices. In every coface of $\sigma$, translation a sufficiently small distance along $d$ changes only the coordinates of vertices of $\sigma$; these remain positive near $x$, all other coordinates remain unchanged, and $r$ changes by exactly that distance. The translations agree on shared faces. Consequently the maps $z\mapsto(z-(r(z)-1/2)d,r(z)-1/2)$ and $(w,s)\mapsto w+sd$ give inverse local piecewise linear product coordinates with $w\in L$. The simplex-link hypothesis supplies the usual local manifold chart for the remaining coordinates. If $x$ is in the interior of $M$, these coordinates identify $V$ locally with a half-space and $L$ with its boundary plane. If $x\in\partial M$, the vector $d$ is tangent to the boundary simplex and these coordinates also preserve $\partial M$; $V$ is locally a quadrant times a line, with its two faces equal to $A$ and $L$.

A quadrant times a line is a piecewise linear half-space: in its two-dimensional factor send the two boundary rays to the positive and negative horizontal rays and send the diagonal ray to the positive vertical ray, extending linearly on the two intervening cones. This is a piecewise linear homeomorphism with piecewise linear inverse, and take its product with the remaining line coordinate. Away from $L$, a point of $V$ has $r>1/2$ and hence inherits the ordinary manifold or boundary chart of $M$. Together with step 3.1 these charts prove that $V$ is a compact piecewise linear three-manifold, $A$ is a subsurface of $\partial M$, and $L$ is a proper piecewise linear surface. At their common points the quadrant model identifies their boundaries with the same line, so their common boundary is exactly $A\cap L$. The finite triangulation of step 2.2 and the deformation retraction of step 2.1 finish the proof. All subdivision, triangulation and coordinate selections are finite.

2. for every vertex $v$ of $K$ the **link graph** $\operatorname{lk}(v)$ — with

([[def-polygonal-schema-and-edge-pairing]]), each of the following operations

1. subdividing a paired side into two sides (edge subdivision);
2. cyclically rotating the boundary word, or reversing the polygon
   orientation and inverting every letter;
3. cancelling an adjacent inverse pair $a\,a^{-1}$ in the boundary word when another paired letter remains; the sole $aa^{-1}$ bigon is the terminal sphere schema and its empty reduced word is notation only;
4. cutting the polygon along an embedded polygonal diagonal whose interior
