derivations.claim: Let $C_*(K)$ be the simplicial chain complex and $C^*(K)$ its vector-space dual, with coboundary $\delta$. Every simplicial one-cocycle $a$ is a coboundary. To prove this, construct a twofold simplicial cover from $a$: its vertices are $(v,\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon\in\mathbb F_2$, its lifted edge over $vw$ goes from $(v,\epsilon)$ to $(w,\epsilon+a(vw))$, and its lifted simplex over a simplex with vertices $v_0,\ldots,v_k$ has labels $\epsilon+a(v_0v_j)$ at $v_j$, with $a(v_0v_0)=0$. The cocycle identity on every triangle makes these prescriptions agree on faces and makes the two lifts of each vertex star disjoint copies of that star. Their realization is a genuine twofold covering space of $V$. If it were connected, it would contradict the hypothesis. Otherwise it has exactly two connected components, each projecting homeomorphically to $V$: path lifting connects a chosen fiber point to one point in every other fiber; if the same component contained both points of one fiber, it would contain both points of every fiber and the whole cover would be connected. Choose one component. The label $b(v)$ of its unique vertex over $v$ satisfies $a(vw)=b(v)+b(w)$, so $a=\delta b$. Thus $H^1(C^*(K))=0$.

Write $d_j:C_j(K)\to C_{j-1}(K)$ for the finite boundary matrices. Gaussian elimination, always taking the first available pivot in the fixed ordering, proves that a matrix and its transpose have the same rank. Consequently $$\dim H_1(C_*(K))=\dim C_1-\operatorname{rank}d_1-\operatorname{rank}d_2=\dim H^1(C^*(K))=0.$$ Thus $H_1(V;\mathbb F_2)=0$ by [F1]. No infinite basis or extension of a functional is selected.

For the finite triangulation fixed in step 1.1, there is also a relative dual-cell decomposition of $(V,\partial V)$. For a $k$-simplex $\sigma$ of $K$, let $B_\sigma$ be the closed union of barycentric simplices whose defining face chain begins with $\sigma$, together with all their faces. Its coface poset identifies it piecewise linearly with the cone on the barycentric subdivision of $\operatorname{lk}(\sigma,K)$. Hence it is a $(3-k)$-ball by the simplex-link hypothesis. For an interior simplex its boundary is the union of the blocks $B_\tau$ for proper cofaces $\tau\supsetneq\sigma$. For a boundary simplex its boundary additionally contains its side in $\partial V$: in the cone-on-ball model that side is the cone on the boundary of the link ball. The boundary side and the coface blocks are the two parts of its ball boundary. The interiors of the blocks off $\partial V$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $V\setminus\partial V$. Indeed, the least face with positive barycentric-chain coordinate determines the unique block interior, while a point whose chain lies wholly in $\partial V$ belongs to the boundary subcomplex. Starting with a finite triangulation of $\partial V$ and attaching these blocks in increasing dimension therefore gives a finite relative CW decomposition of $(V,\partial V)$.

Its relative cellular boundary is $$\partial B_\sigma=\sum_{\substack{\tau\supset\sigma\\\dim\tau=k+1}}B_\tau\quad\pmod{\partial V}.$$ Each listed block is an embedded codimension-one facet of $B_\sigma$ and occurs once. All other boundary faces have smaller dimension or lie in $\partial V$. Equivalently, in its barycentric triangulation the faces obtained by omitting an intermediate chain member cancel in pairs, and the uncanceled faces are precisely those with the least member replaced by an immediate coface; boundary-side faces are zero in the relative complex. Thus the basis correspondence from the cochain dual to $\sigma$ to $B_\sigma$ identifies $C^k(K)$, with coboundary, with the degree-reversed relative dual-cell complex in degree $3-k$. By [F1], this gives $$H_2(V,\partial V;\mathbb F_2)\cong H^1(C^*(K))=0.$$ This is a finite chain-matrix duality calculation, not an invocation of a general Poincaré duality theorem.

The portion $H_2(V,\partial V;\mathbb F_2)\to H_1(\partial V;\mathbb F_2)\to H_1(V;\mathbb F_2)$ of the exact sequence in [F1] now has zero outer groups. Therefore $H_1(\partial V;\mathbb F_2)=0$. In particular this holds for each boundary component, since the finite boundary chain complex is the direct sum of its component complexes. Each component is a closed orientable finite PL surface.

For completeness, apply the finite surface procedure [F2] to such a component $S$. Coherent triangle orientations give opposite directions on the two occurrences of every paired polygon side. Cancel adjacent inverse pairs, retaining the terminal sphere bigon. If an uncanceled residue is nonempty and is not that bigon, it has interlaced pairs: otherwise all pairing chords on its boundary circle would be noncrossing, and an innermost chord would give an adjacent inverse pair. Extract an interlaced pair as a commutator block using [F2]'s explicit cut-and-merge identity, reserve that block, and repeat on the residue. Each cancellation deletes a pair, and each extraction removes two pairs from the unprocessed residue, so this terminates with either the sphere bigon or a product of $g\ge1$ commutator blocks. All cuts and disk identifications are polygonal, and their parametrizations are PL by the disk-extension clause of [F2], so the resulting model is PL homeomorphic to $S$.

A nonempty commutator model has one vertex, $2g$ one-cells, and one two-cell. Its first boundary is zero and its second boundary is zero modulo two, since every side occurs twice. Hence its first homology has dimension $2g>0$ by [F1], contrary to step 4.1. The only remaining model is the sphere bigon, whose quotient is the standard PL two-sphere; one may subdivide its two boundary arcs and realize it as two polygonal disks glued along their common boundary. Thus every component is a PL sphere. All covers, blocks, reductions and pivots used finite data; no arbitrary-index or countable choice was required.

All arcs and graphs in this lemma are finite and polygonal: their edges have disjoint interiors except at specified shared endpoints. A simple polygon separates the plane into one bounded and one unbounded component; the closure of the bounded component is a disk. A prescribed piecewise-linear homeomorphism between the boundaries of two such disks extends to a piecewise-linear homeomorphism of the disks, with piecewise-linear inverse after finite subdivisions.

A finite embedded arc has a disk neighbourhood made from vertex disks and edge strips. Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $G$ be a group and let $N\le G$ be a subgroup ([[def-subgroup]]). For
$g\in G$, write

$$gNg^{-1}:=\{gng^{-1}:n\in N\}.$$

The subgroup $N$ is **normal in $G$** when

$$gNg^{-1}=N\qquad\text{for every }g\in G.$$

In that case write $N\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}G$. Equivalently, every inner
conjugation of $G$ maps $N$ onto itself. The connection with equality of the
left and right cosets of [[def-coset]] is proved in
[[thm-normal-subgroup-characterisations]].

derivations.claim: Each double circle has two distinct preimage circles in $D$, and its normal crossing neighborhood is a product of that circle with a planar cross. To check the possible monodromy, orient $D$ and $M$. Each sheet has its induced coorientation, and the ordered pair of sheet coorientations orients their intersection line. If continuation once around the double circle interchanged the sheets, this orientation of the intersection line would be reversed, which is impossible on a circle. Thus the two sheets return individually. The orientation of each sheet and of the intersection line also preserves each of its transverse directions; consequently no pair of opposite arms is interchanged. Trivializing the interval strips in the two sheets therefore gives the product cross. No rotation or reflection monodromy remains.

The two preimage circles of a chosen double circle bound disks $D_1,D_2\subset D$ by [F1]. If they are nested, say $D_1\subset\operatorname{Int}D_2$, replace the part $D_2$ by a copy of $D_1$, matching boundary points with the same image under $f$, and retain the outside of $D_2$. If they are disjoint, interchange the maps on $D_1$ and $D_2$, with those same boundary identifications, and retain the rest. The identifications extend over the disks by [F1]. At the joining circle resolve the crossing by connecting adjacent arms of the planar cross instead of opposite arms. The resolution can be made polygonal: in a small square normal section replace the two crossing segments by two disjoint bent polygonal arcs joining the selected adjacent pairs, equal to the old arms near the square boundary. Taking products with successive subintervals of the double circle gives matching polygonal annuli; step 1.1 ensures their end identifications agree. This removes that double circle. The retained domain is a disk, its external boundary map is unchanged, and each retained old sheet piece is used at most once. Outside the crossing neighborhood no new double value is introduced; inside it the replacement sheets are disjoint. Other double curves miss this neighborhood and are either retained or discarded.

Repeat step 2.1 until there are no double circles. The number of double curves strictly decreases at every repetition and was finite initially. Each new disk is still a proper polygonal immersion with at most two preimages per value, regular double arcs, and the original boundary loop. The intermediate disk need not lift to an embedding in any covering space; this proof concerns the immersion in $M$ itself.

Choose a double arc $C$. Its two preimage arcs $a,b$ are disjoint proper arcs in the disk. They cut it into three polygonal disks, in order an outer piece, a middle piece, and the other outer piece. Orient the boundary of $D$, and label its four successive portions by $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ so that $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are the exposed boundary intervals of the outer pieces. The two ways of matching the orientations of $a$ and $b$ give the following boundary words after the two possible crossing resolutions: $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} &\text{original}&\text{first disk}&\text{second disk}\\ \text{same orientation}&\alpha\beta\gamma\delta&\alpha\gamma&\alpha\beta^{-1}\gamma\delta^{-1}\\ \text{opposite orientations}&\alpha\beta\gamma\delta&\alpha\gamma^{-1}&\alpha\delta\gamma\beta\end{array}.$$ Here all boundary paths are their images in $F$; short joining paths inside the endpoint half-disk neighborhoods have been collapsed in the written words. They are homotopic to the actual polygonal boundary paths. To verify the domains and the words, cut along $a,b$, and use the common parametrization of their images $C$ to match the cut shores. Joining the two outer disks along one shore produces the first disk, with the exposed intervals $\alpha,\gamma$ read in the matching directions. Joining all three disks in the other order along two shores produces the second disk; following its boundary reads the remaining word in the table. Each join is along a full boundary interval, hence gives a disk by [F1]. Each old piece is used at most once in either candidate. This surgery will be applied after the circle eliminations of step 3.1.

Realize each of these two gluings in $M$ by the corresponding adjacent-arm resolution along $C$. In a transverse square use the two disjoint bent arcs described in step 2.1. At an endpoint use its half-space version; the changed boundary arcs stay in $F$, since that endpoint has a neighborhood in the subsurface containing the original boundary germs. Subdivide finitely along $C$ to obtain polygonal product strips, and use a width smaller than their positive distances to all other double curves and to nonincident sheet pieces. Thus the replacement is a proper polygonal immersion with no double value along $C$ and with no newly introduced double curve. Away from the strip it uses a subset of the old sheet pieces, with no repetition. The two-to-one bound is therefore preserved. The remaining double curves are among the old ones other than $C$.

At least one candidate disk still has its boundary class outside $N$. In the first row of the table put $w=\alpha\beta\gamma\delta$, $u=\alpha\gamma$, $v=\alpha\beta^{-1}\gamma\delta^{-1}$. Cancellation of successive reversed paths gives $$w=u\delta^{-1}v^{-1}u\delta.$$ In the second row put $u=\alpha\gamma^{-1}$ and $v=\alpha\delta\gamma\beta$. Then the corresponding cancellation identity is $$w=u(\gamma\delta)^{-1}u^{-1}v(\gamma\delta).$$ These are identities of composable paths with the indicated common endpoint identifications; inserting basepaths turns them into products of conjugates in $\pi_1(F)$. By [F2], if both candidate boundary classes belonged to $N$, so would $w$, contradicting the induction hypothesis. Retain a candidate whose boundary class is outside $N$.

Repeat steps 4.1–6.1. Each repetition removes at least one double arc and introduces none, so after finitely many repetitions there is a proper polygonal immersion of a disk with no double values and with boundary class outside $N$. It is injective. A continuous injection of the compact disk into the Hausdorff manifold $M$ is an embedding; its polygonal local models make this a piecewise linear proper embedding. Its boundary is in $F$, as required. All choices made in the construction are finite; no countable or arbitrary-index choice assumption has been used.

citations.quote: Let $K$ be finite, $A\subseteq K$ and $B\subseteq L$ subcomplexes, and $f:(|K|,|A|)\to(|L|,|B|)$ continuous. For all sufficiently large integers $r$, there is a simplicial approximation $g:(\operatorname{sd}^rK,\operatorname{sd}^rA)\to(L,B)$, homotopic as a map of pairs to $f b_K^r$. Here $b_K^r$ is the composite barycentric homeomorphism. No pointwise fixing of a positive-dimensional restriction is asserted.

Let $M$ be a compact piecewise linear three-manifold, possibly with boundary, equipped with a finite triangulation in which the boundary is a subcomplex and simplex links have the standard sphere or ball forms. Let $P$ be a subcomplex and let $W$ be any relatively open neighborhood of $|P|$ in $M$. There is a compact piecewise linear three-manifold $V\subset W$, with $|P|\subset\operatorname{Int}_M V$, such that $V$ strongly deformation retracts onto $|P|$. It has a finite triangulation extending a subdivision of $P$. Its trace $V\cap\partial M$ is a compact piecewise linear subsurface of $\partial M$, and its remaining frontier is a properly embedded piecewise linear surface; these surfaces meet along their common boundary. The trace may be empty. If $|P|$ is connected, $V$ is connected.

Let $P$ be a compact subpolyhedron of a polyhedron $Q$. Suppose $P$ is locally piecewise linearly collared in $Q$: each point has a product neighborhood in which $P$ is the bottom of a piecewise linear product with $[0,1)$. Then there is a piecewise linear embedding $c:P\times[0,1]\to Q$ with $c(x,0)=x$ such that $c(P\times[0,1))$ is an open neighborhood of $P$ in $Q$. In particular the boundary of every compact piecewise linear manifold has such a collar.

Let $Y$ be path-connected and locally path-connected, let $f:(Y,y_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be based, and let $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ be a covering. A based lift $\widetilde f:(Y,y_0)\to(E,e_0)$ exists if and only if $f_*\pi_1(Y,y_0)\subseteq p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$; when it exists it is unique.

Let $V$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a finite compatible triangulation $K$, with boundary a subcomplex, and with every simplex link a standard piecewise linear sphere or ball of the appropriate dimension. If $V$ has no connected twofold covering space, every connected component of $\partial V$ is piecewise linearly homeomorphic to the standard two-sphere. This conclusion uses only finite simplicial and cellular calculations and has no choice hypothesis.

A simple polygon separates the plane into one bounded and one unbounded component; the closure of the bounded component is a disk. A prescribed piecewise-linear homeomorphism between the boundaries of two such disks extends to a piecewise-linear homeomorphism of the disks, with piecewise-linear inverse after finite subdivisions.

A finite connected plane graph has a compact disk-and-band neighbourhood; filling its bounded complementary boundary circles produces a closed disk. Subdividing an edge does not change these conclusions. Loops use two distinct attachment germs. No ambient-plane extension is asserted.

Let $M$ be an orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with boundary, let $F$ be a connected subsurface of its boundary, and let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $\pi_1(F)$. Suppose $f:D\to M$ is a proper piecewise linear immersion of a finite polygonal disk, with $f(\partial D)\subset F$, having only regular double curves and with no point having more than two inverse images. More precisely, the double-value set is a finite disjoint union of circles in the interior and arcs properly ending in the boundary; near a double value the two sheets are transverse planes, or transverse half-planes at an endpoint, and there are no other singularities. If the boundary loop of $f$ does not represent an element of $N$, then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $F$ and does not represent an element of $N$.

Membership in $N$ for an unbased boundary loop is interpreted after joining it to a fixed basepoint in $F$. It is independent of that joining path because $N$ is normal. The disk produced need not have the same boundary as $f$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], replace $f$ by a PL map with boundary homotopic to the original one in $F$. Choose the approximation sufficiently fine on its compact boundary image to keep that image in $\operatorname{Int}F$. Make the map proper without changing its boundary: in a boundary collar $c(u,s)$, a push with parameter $a\ge0$ replaces the height $s$ by $\max(s,a)$ for $s$ below the collar top and is the identity elsewhere, with $a$ smaller than that top. This is a continuous PL function jointly in $(s,a)$. Choose a nonnegative PL function $a$ on the source disk, zero precisely on its boundary and everywhere sufficiently small, and apply that push to the value of the map at each point. Its straight parameter interpolation gives a homotopy relative to the source boundary. After compatible subdivisions the resulting proper PL map $f_0:D\to M$ is simplicial for one fixed finite triangulation of $D$. Its boundary class is still outside $N$. Put $D_0=f_0(D)$ and use [F2] to choose a connected compact manifold neighborhood $V_0$ retracting onto $D_0$ whose trace in $\partial M$ lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$. Let $F_0$ be the component of that trace containing $f_0(\partial D)$.

If $V_0$ has a connected twofold cover $p_1:M_1\to V_0$, lift $f_0$ to $f_1:D\to M_1$ by [F4], put $D_1=f_1(D)$, and choose by [F2] a connected compact manifold neighborhood $V_1$ retracting onto $D_1$. Its trace is chosen inside the relative interior of $p_1^{-1}(F_0)$; let $F_1$ be the component containing $f_1(\partial D)$. Repeat whenever $V_i$ has a connected twofold cover. Write $q_i:V_i\to M$ for the composite of the covers and neighborhood inclusions. Then $q_if_i=f_0$, $q_i(F_i)\subset F$, and $N_i=(q_i|_{F_i})_*^{-1}(N)$ is normal. The boundary class of $f_i$ is outside $N_i$ at every stage. Orientability and the finite compatible PL structures pass to the covers and the neighborhoods.

This tower is finite. Give $D_i$ the simplicial structure obtained by lifting the original image simplices of $D_0$, irrespective of any additional subdivisions used for $V_i$. Its number of simplices is at most the number of simplices in the fixed source disk: each image simplex is the image of at least one source simplex, and each such source simplex has just one lift in the image of $f_i$. Let $\tau_i$ be the deck involution of $p_i$. The inverse image of $D_{i-1}$ is $D_i\cup\tau_i(D_i)$: every point of $D_{i-1}$ is hit by $f_{i-1}$ and its two lifts are interchanged by $\tau_i$. This inverse image is connected, because lifting the deformation retraction of $V_{i-1}$ onto $D_{i-1}$ retracts the connected $M_i$ onto it. The two finite closed sets $D_i$ and $\tau_i(D_i)$ must therefore meet. Since their union is a lifted simplicial complex, their intersection contains a common simplex. Thus $\tau_i$ identifies two distinct simplices of $D_i$ under projection; they are distinct because a deck transformation fixing a simplex would fix its barycenter. Projection takes $D_i$ onto $D_{i-1}$, so $D_i$ has strictly more simplices than $D_{i-1}$. This strict increase is bounded by the fixed finite source count. We reach a last $V_n$ with no connected twofold cover.

Apply [F5] to the last $V_n$ of step 3.1. It has the required finite compatible PL manifold triangulation and orientation by step 2.1 and has no connected twofold cover. Therefore each component of $\partial V_n$ is a PL two-sphere. In particular the endpoint argument uses no general Poincaré duality theorem, singular UCT splitting or unrestricted surface-classification hypothesis; their required finite calculations have been proved in [F5].

The marked $F_n$ is a compact connected subsurface of one of these spheres. It is planar. Its fundamental group is normally generated by its boundary circles: join its finitely many complementary disk regions by disjoint polygonal arcs in the sphere; cutting along the corresponding arcs in $F_n$ gives a polygonal disk, and identifying its paired cut shores expresses each loop as a product of conjugates of boundary loops. The same conclusion follows by collapsing those cut arcs to a finite tree; the unfilled boundary circles supply the remaining generators. If $F_n$ is the whole sphere, its fundamental group is trivial, contradicting the boundary class of $f_n$ being outside $N_n$. Hence some boundary component of $F_n$ has class outside $N_n$. Move it slightly into $\operatorname{Int}F_n$ using [F3], without changing its free homotopy class, and call the resulting embedded polygonal circle $C$. By the PL sphere model of [F6] and the polygonal disk construction there, $C$ bounds a PL disk in $\partial V_n$. Push this disk into $V_n$ relative to $C$ by its boundary collar: in that collar use the graph of a small PL function on the disk, positive on its interior and zero on its boundary. The graph is embedded and proper and is PL after subdivision. We obtain a proper PL embedded disk $g_n:D\to V_n$ with boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F_n$ outside $N_n$.

Suppose a proper PL embedded disk $g_i:D\to V_i$ has been obtained with its boundary class outside $N_i$. Regard it in $M_i$ and perturb it into general position with its deck translate, using the following finite vertex-push construction. Cover its compact image and its translate by finitely many linear coordinate balls $U$ with $U\cap\tau_iU=\varnothing$, together with boundary half-balls. In each ball triangulate the compact disk pieces and the ambient ball, shift one disk vertex a sufficiently small distance, and extend the move by coning to the fixed boundary of its ambient vertex star. The cone construction gives an ambient PL homeomorphism; the disk therefore remains embedded. In $U$, a move of $g_i$ supported in $U$ leaves $\tau_i g_i$ fixed, since that translate changes only in $\tau_iU$. Choose the finitely many shifts in general affine position relative to the fixed translated simplices. Each excluded affine dependence is a proper determinant zero set, so the allowed small open parameter box contains a choice outside their finite union. Applying $\tau_i$ shows that the paired intersection in $\tau_iU$ is also in general position. Process the finite chart pairs in order, retaining the previously treated compact pieces; later moves can be taken sufficiently small to preserve the finitely many nonzero determinants and positive separations already obtained. First do the boundary in its two-dimensional charts, and extend its moves over a small collar by [F3]; then do the interiors relative to that collar. The resulting intersections avoid sheet vertices and pairs of sheet edges. An intersection across one sheet edge and a face of the other has two incident intersection segments, and a face-face intersection is a transverse segment. Thus the double-value set is a disjoint finite union of regular polygonal circles and proper arcs, with the transverse half-plane model at their endpoints. There are no triple values because $g_i$ is embedded and $p_i$ has two sheets. The boundary motions are homotopies in the open marked surface and preserve the class modulo $N_i$. This construction uses only PL coordinate charts and cone moves, without assuming a smoothing of $M_i$.

Apply [F7] in the orientable $V_{i-1}$ to $p_i g_i$ and the normal subgroup $N_{i-1}$. Its boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F_{i-1}$ by the marked-neighborhood construction. Its boundary class is outside $N_{i-1}$ because its further image in $F$ is outside $N$. Thus [F7] gives a properly embedded PL disk $g_{i-1}$ with boundary class outside $N_{i-1}$. Every boundary surgery can be kept inside the open marked surface, so its boundary still lies in $\operatorname{Int}F_{i-1}$. Repeat steps 6.1–7.1 down the finite tower. No embeddedness of an intermediate disk lift is assumed after the double-curve surgeries; at the end of each descent step [F7] gives a new embedded disk, which is the input to the next descent.

We finish with a proper PL embedded disk $g_0$ in $V_0$. Its interior is disjoint from $\partial V_0$, hence from $\partial M$, while its boundary lies in $F_0\subset\operatorname{Int}F$; it is therefore a proper embedded disk in $M$. Its boundary class maps outside $N$ by definition of $N_0$. For the final particular case, take $F$ to be the indicated boundary component and $N$ the trivial subgroup. A nontrivial element of the kernel has a nullhomotopy disk, and the preceding argument gives an embedded disk whose boundary is still nontrivial in that component. This proves the theorem. Every tower has the finite bound proved in step 3.1, and all perturbation, surgery and matrix choices are finite. No countable or arbitrary-index choice hypothesis is introduced.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a compact piecewise linear three-manifold, possibly with boundary, equipped with a finite triangulation in which the boundary is a subcomplex and simplex links have the standard sphere or ball forms. Let $P$ be a subcomplex and let $W$ be any relatively open neighborhood of $|P|$ in $M$. There is a compact piecewise linear three-manifold $V\subset W$, with $|P|\subset\operatorname{Int}_M V$, such that $V$ strongly deformation retracts onto $|P|$. It has a finite triangulation extending a subdivision of $P$. Its trace $V\cap\partial M$ is a compact piecewise linear subsurface of $\partial M$, and its remaining frontier is a properly embedded piecewise linear surface; these surfaces meet along their common boundary. The trace may be empty. If $|P|$ is connected, $V$ is connected.

Let $P$ be a compact subpolyhedron of a polyhedron $Q$. Suppose $P$ is locally piecewise linearly collared in $Q$: each point has a product neighborhood in which $P$ is the bottom of a piecewise linear product with $[0,1)$. Then there is a piecewise linear embedding $c:P\times[0,1]\to Q$ with $c(x,0)=x$ such that $c(P\times[0,1))$ is an open neighborhood of $P$ in $Q$. In particular the boundary of every compact piecewise linear manifold has such a collar.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

All arcs and graphs in this lemma are finite and polygonal: their edges have disjoint interiors except at specified shared endpoints. A simple polygon separates the plane into one bounded and one unbounded component; the closure of the bounded component is a disk. A prescribed piecewise-linear homeomorphism between the boundaries of two such disks extends to a piecewise-linear homeomorphism of the disks, with piecewise-linear inverse after finite subdivisions.

A finite embedded arc has a disk neighbourhood made from vertex disks and edge strips. A finite connected plane graph has a compact disk-and-band neighbourhood; filling its bounded complementary boundary circles produces a closed disk. Subdividing an edge does not change these conclusions. Loops use two distinct attachment germs. No ambient-plane extension is asserted.

Let $S$ be a nonempty connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]). Let $K$ be a finite abstract
simplicial complex ([[def-abstract-simplicial-complex]]) whose simplices all
have dimension at most $2$, let $h:|K|\to S$ be a homeomorphism, and suppose
that:

1. every $1$-simplex of $K$ is contained in exactly two $2$-simplices of $K$;
2. for every vertex $v$ of $K$ the **link graph** $\operatorname{lk}(v)$ — with
   one vertex for each $1$-simplex $\{v,w\}$ of $K$ and one edge $\{x,y\}$ for
   each $2$-simplex $\{v,x,y\}$ of $K$ — is a cycle.

Then there is a polygonal schema with exactly one polygon
([[def-polygonal-schema-and-edge-pairing]]) whose realization $Y$ is
homeomorphic to $S$.

The construction selects only from finite collections and uses no choice
principle.

For one-polygon surface schemas
([[def-polygonal-schema-and-edge-pairing]]), each of the following operations
preserves the quotient homeomorphism type:

1. subdividing a paired side into two sides (edge subdivision);
2. cyclically rotating the boundary word, or reversing the polygon
   orientation and inverting every letter;
3. cancelling an adjacent inverse pair $a\,a^{-1}$ in the boundary word when another paired letter remains; the sole $aa^{-1}$ bigon is the terminal sphere schema and its empty reduced word is notation only;
4. cutting the polygon along an embedded polygonal diagonal whose interior
   lies in the polygon interior, and regluing the two new boundary sides to
   each other (a $(P2)$ split), as well as the inverse operation of gluing two
   faces along a paired pair of sides.

The resulting finite cut-and-paste identities move two same-direction
occurrences of a letter together as a crosscap block $bb$, extract an
interlaced pair pattern $a\,U\,b\,V\,a^{-1}X\,b^{-1}Y$ as a commutator handle
block $c\,d\,c^{-1}d^{-1}YX\,VU$, and replace one handle plus one crosscap by
three crosscaps. Each move preserves the surface link condition, and no choice
axiom is used.

Let $K$ be finite, $A\subseteq K$ and $B\subseteq L$ subcomplexes, and $f:(|K|,|A|)\to(|L|,|B|)$ continuous. For all sufficiently large integers $r$, there is a simplicial approximation $g:(\operatorname{sd}^rK,\operatorname{sd}^rA)\to(L,B)$, homotopic as a map of pairs to $f b_K^r$. Here $b_K^r$ is the composite barycentric homeomorphism. No pointwise fixing of a positive-dimensional restriction is asserted.

derivations.claim: We shall use compact PL neighborhoods in open parts of $X$. The construction in [F1] applies to a compact set inside such a part even though $X$ is not compact. Indeed, local finiteness and compactness give a finite union of closed simplex stars containing that set in its relative interior. Subdivide this finite union sufficiently finely that a further closed star neighborhood stays in the specified open part; compactness gives the required positive separation in any of the finitely many local realization metrics. For a resulting finite subcomplex $P$, make it full by one barycentric subdivision and use $r$, the sum of barycentric coordinates at its vertices, to form $\{r\ge1/2\}$. The support of $r$ lies in the finite union of stars incident to those vertices, so this neighborhood is compact. The translation charts and retraction formulas in [F1] verify its manifold structure and marked boundary traces without using any simplex outside that finite union. If connectedness is needed, connect the finitely many components of the chosen finite subcomplex by finitely many PL paths first.

Enlarge the given $A$ to a compact connected PL core $A_0$ containing both $A$ and $\partial X$ in its relative interior, using step 1.1. Apply end condition 2 to $A_0$, obtaining a compact $C\supset A_0$ outside which every loop contracts in $X\setminus A_0$. Choose a compact connected PL core $N_0$ containing $C$ in its relative interior and containing $\partial X$. Its frontier $S_0=\partial N_0\setminus\partial X$ is a finite disjoint union of closed orientable PL surfaces in $\operatorname{Int}X$, disjoint from $C$. Every loop of $S_0$ therefore contracts in $X\setminus A_0$.

Suppose a compact PL core $N$ containing $A_0$ has frontier $S$ disjoint from $A_0$, every loop of $S$ contracts in $X\setminus A_0$, and a component of $S$ has positive genus. We produce a compression disk outside $A_0$. Choose a nontrivial polygonal loop on that component using its finite disk-and-band model in [F4], and choose a nullhomotopy in $X\setminus A_0$. Its compact image and $S$ lie in a compact PL manifold neighborhood $Y\subset X\setminus A_0$ by step 1.1. Approximate the map piecewise linearly by [F5] and put it transverse to $S$: subdivide its finite triangles in the product charts of the two-sided $S$ and choose vertex heights avoiding zero; the zero-height segments form a finite collection of simple polygonal circles in the source interior, in addition to its boundary. If such an interior preimage circle gives a trivial loop in $S$, replace its entire inside map by a nullhomotopy in $S$ pushed to the side occupied by its outside collar. The target side collar exists by [F2] after cutting $Y$ along $S$. Moving the source circle slightly to that side removes it and all circles inside it, introducing none. Repeat finitely. An innermost remaining circle, allowing the source boundary itself, now bounds a disk map whose interior misses $S$ and whose boundary is nontrivial on $S$. It lies in one of the compact pieces obtained by cutting $Y$ along $S$. Apply [F3] to that piece and its marked copy of $S$. The resulting properly embedded PL disk $D$ has interior disjoint from $S$, boundary essential on $S$, and is disjoint from $A_0$.

Compress $S$ along $D$ and update $N$. The disk has a product neighborhood relative to its boundary: in a finite PL disk the local links are polygonal circles or arcs in the ambient link sphere or disk, and [F4]'s disk parametrizations flatten them. After cutting along the disk, [F2] supplies its two side collars, giving $D\times[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$ when they are glued back. Choose it disjoint from $A_0$. If $D$ lies outside $N$, attach this two-handle to $N$; if it lies inside, remove its open product neighborhood. Keep the component containing the connected $A_0$ and discard any others. In either case the new core still contains $A_0$ and has the compressed surface as its frontier, possibly with some components discarded. Every loop on the new frontier is still nullhomotopic in $X\setminus A_0$: perturb it off the centers of the finitely many new cap disks, then push each portion in a punctured cap to its boundary circle. It becomes a loop on the old frontier, and these pushes take place outside $A_0$.

The operation terminates after finitely many applications. Give a closed orientable surface of genus $g>0$ the complexity $2g-1$, and give a sphere complexity zero; sum over frontier components. These are finite integers by [F4]. A nonseparating compression decreases genus by one; a separating essential compression splits a genus $g$ component into genera $g_1,g_2\ge1$ with $g_1+g_2=g$. These assertions follow directly by cutting the disk-and-band polygon along the essential curve and capping its two new boundary circles; an essential separating curve has positive genus on both sides, since a genus-zero side with one boundary is a disk. Thus the complexity decreases by at least one, also in the case $g=1$ yielding a sphere. Discarding components cannot increase it. Repeating steps 3.1–4.1 produces a compact connected PL core $N$ containing $A_0$ and with frontier a finite union of PL two-spheres.

There are finitely many complementary components: each has at least one of those finitely many frontier spheres in its boundary, and each sphere is incident to just one outside component. End condition 1 says precisely one component has noncompact closure. Adjoin the closures of all other components to $N$. Their union is compact, since there are finitely many and each closure is compact. The adjunction is along complete boundary components and preserves the PL manifold structure and connectedness. The resulting compact core still contains $A_0$, its frontier is still a finite union of spheres, and its exterior is connected with noncompact closure. There is at least one frontier sphere: otherwise this nonempty compact codimension-zero core would be both open and closed in the connected noncompact $X$.

If more than one frontier sphere remains, join two of them by a proper embedded polygonal arc in the connected exterior, with interior in the exterior interior. Such an arc exists: take a finite polygonal path, erase its closed subpaths, and perturb its finitely many remaining segments in three-dimensional charts to avoid self-intersections. It has a product neighborhood $D^2\times[0,1]$, with its end disks in those two spheres. Construct it from disjoint small coordinate balls at its successive vertices and thin boxes along its edges; the polygonal disk extension in [F4] matches their transverse disk coordinates successively along the interval, so no transition obstruction occurs. Attach this one-handle to the core. Its two end disks are removed from the frontier spheres and joined by a cylinder; the result is a single PL sphere, since each punctured sphere is a polygonal disk and their connecting cylinder gives the standard two-disk sphere model. The exterior stays connected: any finite path between two points may be perturbed off the arc, and its portions in the small tube may then be pushed to the tube frontier; this uses only avoidance of finitely many line segments in three-dimensional boxes. Repeat finitely until there is one frontier sphere. The final core is the required $K$, since all alterations were outside $A_0$ and hence preserve the original $A$ in its relative interior. The entire construction uses finitely many nullhomotopy, disk, path and coordinate choices, with the finite bound in step 5.1; no countable or arbitrary-index choice hypothesis is introduced.

Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. Choose one relative interior point in each nonempty cell; triangulate the boundary in increasing dimension and cone from that point. This construction agrees on every common face and preserves each cell as a subpolyhedron.

Let $Q$ be a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron with a fixed finite linear triangulation $T$. If $f:P\to Q$ is a piecewise-linear embedding of a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron, then some finite subdivision $T'$ of $T$ contains $f(P)$ as the realization of a subcomplex.

Let $P$ be a compact subpolyhedron of a polyhedron $Q$. Suppose $P$ is locally piecewise linearly collared in $Q$: each point has a product neighborhood in which $P$ is the bottom of a piecewise linear product with $[0,1)$. derivations.claim: We first establish the boundary-disk fact needed for (a): the closure of the complement of a parametrized PL disk $D$ in the boundary $S$ of a parametrized three-ball is another parametrized PL disk. Use the supplied ball parameter to replace $S$ by the boundary of a tetrahedron. This replacement is legitimate for any convex polyhedral ball model: triangulate its boundary and the tetrahedral boundary, choose an interior point in each, and cone a boundary parameter when available; alternatively a direct radial face subdivision identifies the two convex boundaries, since each ray from an interior point has one endpoint on each boundary. To verify that last identification is PL, subdivide both radial face decompositions into their common polyhedral cones, take their sections, and map corresponding sections by face-compatible coning; no assertion that the radial formula itself is affine is needed. Pick a point off $D$. A finite succession of small PL disk-chart point pushes on $S$ sends it to a tetrahedral vertex $q$: choose a polygonal path to $q$, cover it by finitely many small polygonal charts, and in each chart triangulate a convex polygon as a fan from the current point and move the fan center to the next nearby point, fixing the polygon boundary. These affine triangle maps give the required point push and inverse. After this boundary homeomorphism, $q\notin D$. Choose a small triangular section $\Gamma$ of the cone at $q$ whose closed cone misses $D$. The closure $K$ of the rest of the tetrahedral boundary consists of the opposite face $T$ and the three quadrilateral strips between $\partial T$ and $\Gamma$. It has an explicit PL parameter as a larger planar triangle: send $T$ to a smaller concentric triangle and the three strips to the corresponding trapezoids of the surrounding planar triangular annulus. On every strip prescribe its four boundary sides linearly after subdivision and extend by [F1]. The maps agree on shared sides. Thus $K$ is a planar polygonal disk containing $D$ away from its boundary.

In this planar parameter, $\partial D$ is a simple polygon. Its bounded side is precisely $D$. Indeed the interior of the embedded disk is open on the local interior side of its polygonal boundary: at an interior simplex this follows from its planar triangle star, and at boundary simplices from the half-disk fan. It is also closed relative to the polygon complement, since $D$ is compact. Its connected interior therefore fills one component of that complement; it is bounded and hence fills the bounded component by [F1]. The region between $D$ and the outer triangle is a parametrized PL annulus. Here is an explicit disk reduction: choose an embedded polygonal arc joining the two boundaries, with interior disjoint from both, by a finite chain of triangles of a compatible triangulation; delete loops from the finite edge path and perturb it off boundary edges. A narrow polygonal strip along this arc joins the two boundaries. The closure of the remaining region is a polygonal disk: its boundary traces the outer boundary, one strip shore, the inner boundary in reverse, and the other shore, with no repeated vertices except its closing endpoint. [F1] parametrizes that disk and extends any prescribed boundary map respecting this cyclic order. Match it to a rectangle cut open along one spanning strip in a standard polygonal annulus, then restore the strip by its disk boundary-extension map. Thus the annulus has a PL parameter with its two boundary circles prescribed. Glue its inner boundary to the disk $q*\Gamma$. A polygonal annulus glued to a polygonal disk along its inner boundary is a polygonal disk: in the standard annulus parameter fill its inner polygon using [F1]. This gives a finite PL parameter of $\overline{S\setminus D}$. This argument also proves extension of any prescribed boundary map between the complementary disks, by applying [F1] in their disk parameters.

For (a), extend $f|_{\partial D_1}$ over the complementary disks furnished by step 2.1. Paste this extension with $f$ to obtain a PL homeomorphism $\partial B_1\to\partial B_2$. Transfer it by the supplied ball parameters to the boundaries of convex polyhedral balls. Subdivide until that boundary map is affine on every boundary triangle and cone these triangles from an interior point in each ball. The affine maps of corresponding tetrahedra match on faces and are bijective, since the cones cover each ball with disjoint interiors. They give the extension and a PL inverse. This proves (a). For (b), apply (a) to send the two marked balls to $[-1,0]\times[-1,1]^2$ and $[0,1]\times[-1,1]^2$, taking their attaching disks to the common square and their specified attaching map to its identity. The resulting quotient is the rectangular box $[-1,1]\times[-1,1]^2$, with the finite compatible PL parameter obtained by gluing these maps.

Now assume (c), and put $F=\overline{\partial A\setminus D}$. It is a parametrized disk by step 2.1. The space $Q=\overline{B\setminus A}$ is locally a PL three-manifold with boundary. At a point of $F\setminus C$, take a compatible finite triangulation for the ambient ball chart and the supplied parameter of $A$. Its ambient link is a standard PL two-sphere and its link on the $A$ side is a parametrized disk: this follows by subdividing the local PL ball parameter until it is linear on the incident simplices. The complementary link disk is supplied by steps 1.1–2.1. Parametrize those two disks compatibly on their common circle, using [F1], to identify the link pair with two standard hemispherical disks. Coning this link identification gives the local half-ball chart on the $Q$ side and a product collar of $F$. Elsewhere away from $C$ the ordinary interior charts of $B\setminus A$ or boundary charts of $B$ apply. Along $C$ the given window chart identifies $Q$ with the quadrant $v\ge0,w\ge0$; subdivision into finitely many angular sectors flattens that quadrant to a half-space. In these same charts $F$ is the face $v=0,w\ge0$. It is locally PL collared in $Q$, including along $\partial F=C$, where its local collar is the quadrant product. Consequently [F3] gives $c:F\times[0,1]\to Q$ with bottom $F$ and half-open image a neighborhood of $F$. Its side $c(C\times[0,1])$ lies in $\partial B$. To check this last assertion, the local product has boundary $C\times[0,1)$ away from the bottom, while the boundary of $Q$ off $F$ is $\partial B\setminus D$; PL local charts distinguish boundary points by their ball or half-ball links. The top side follows by continuity. Thus $N=A\cup c(F\times[0,1])$ is a neighborhood of $A$ in $B$ whose relative frontier is the outer disk $c(F\times\{1\})$.

Give $A$ a PL parameter as a convex pyramid $P$ with flat base $D_0$, carrying $D$ to that base, by (a). Choose a point $p$ in the relative interior of $D_0$ as follows. The composite of this parameter's inverse with the supplied parameter of $B$ is PL; after a finite common subdivision its restriction near the relative interior of some base triangle lies in a single incident three-simplex and is affine there. Its image base triangle can also be taken inside one flat boundary face of the convex model of $B$. Choose $p$ inside that base triangle, avoiding its edges. For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, the homothetic pyramid $\epsilon P=p+\epsilon(P-p)$ therefore maps affinely into that one boundary three-simplex of $B$. The radial shells between $P$ and $2P=p+2(P-p)$ are finite convex prisms over the free boundary faces of $P$, including their boundary faces on the base. There is a PL homeomorphism $N\to2P$ agreeing with the chosen parameter on $A=P$: on $F\times[0,1]$ map the bottom to the free face of $P$ and the top to its doubled face, and fill the corresponding face prisms compatibly. More explicitly, first prescribe all vertex and boundary face maps, then extend over each convex cell by coning its already parametrized boundary to an interior point. Both sides are convex cells with corresponding faces, so the resulting map is bijective with PL inverse. This is a finite prism construction using [F2], not the generally non-PL radial interpolation formula.

Construct a PL self-homeomorphism of $2P$ taking $P$ to $\epsilon P$ and fixing its outer free boundary. On $P$ use the affine homothety of ratio $\epsilon$ about $p$. On each shell prism between a free face of $P$ and its doubled face use the corresponding prism between the $\epsilon$-scaled face and the doubled face. Their face structures agree; the finite face-coning construction of step 4.1 extends the prescribed bottom and fixed top maps compatibly. On the base this map carries the base annulus to the corresponding base annulus, and is allowed to move base points. It fixes the relative frontier of $N$ in $B$, so transfer it to $N$ and extend by the identity on $B\setminus\operatorname{Int}_B N$. We obtain a PL homeomorphism $h:B\to B$ taking $A$ to a ball $A_\epsilon$ which, in the supplied convex parameter of $B$, is an affine pyramid with its base in the interior of a flat boundary face and its remaining points inside $B$. In particular $h(Q)=\overline{B\setminus A_\epsilon}$.

The complement of this small affine pyramid has a direct PL parameter as $B$. In its flat boundary chart choose an inward transverse direction along the segment from an interior base point to the pyramid apex. In the resulting oblique coordinates the pyramid is $\{(x,z):x\in D_\epsilon,\ 0\le z\le\phi(x)\}$, where $\phi$ is the nonnegative piecewise affine pyramid roof, zero on $\partial D_\epsilon$. Choose a larger convex polygon $R$ in that flat boundary face, extend $\phi$ by zero on $R\setminus D_\epsilon$, and choose $H>\max\phi$ such that $R\times[0,H]$ lies in the boundary chart in $B$. These choices can be made by first taking $\epsilon$ sufficiently small: the affine pyramid shrinks to the interior point of a boundary face, where $B$ contains a fixed oblique half-prism. Subdivide $R$ until $\phi$ is affine on each cell. The cells $\{(x,z):x\in\sigma,\ \phi(x)\le z\le H\}$ are convex prisms with the same face incidences as $\sigma\times[0,H]$. Map their graph bottoms to $z=0$ by the identity in $x$, their tops identically, and their side faces compatibly by the finite face-coning construction. Where $\phi=0$ choose the identity throughout. The resulting PL homeomorphism straightens the graph prism onto $R\times[0,H]$, fixes its top and outer sides, and extends by the identity outside that prism. Its domain is exactly $\overline{B\setminus A_\epsilon}$: above an interior base point only the roof and points above it survive the closure, while at the edge of the base $\phi=0$. It therefore gives a finite PL homeomorphism $\overline{B\setminus A_\epsilon}\to B$. Composing with $h|_Q$ proves (c). Only finitely many subdivisions, disk cuts, chart points and convex cell extensions were used, so none of (a)–(c) requires countable or arbitrary-index choice.

derivations.claim: If a cell $C$ meets some level in $[a,b]$, it has vertices strictly below $a$ and strictly above $b$. Indeed the minimum and maximum of the affine function on the convex polytope occur at vertices; a cell meeting the slab cannot have either extremum inside it, by hypothesis. The same holds for every face that meets the slab. Its section $C_t=C\cap\ell^{-1}(t)$ is consequently nonempty for every $t\in[a,b]$ and meets the relative interior of $C$: take an interior point of $C$, and join it to points near the minimum and maximum to obtain interior points below and above $t$, then intersect their segment with the level. In particular no new face begins or ends while the section level traverses this interval.

More precisely, the faces of $C_t$ correspond to the proper faces $G$ of $C$ meeting the slab, together with $C$ itself: intersect each such face with the level and retain the empty face separately. Every face of the section is of this form because an exposing affine functional on its hyperplane extends to the ambient affine span and its maximizing face on the section is cut out by a collection of the supporting facet equations of $C$. The correspondence is injective: $G_t$ meets the relative interior of $G$ by step 1.1, so its smallest containing face of $C$ is $G$. It preserves inclusions and is independent of $t$. The faces of the truncated cell $\widehat C=C\cap\ell^{-1}([a,b])$ are its bottom and top sections and the truncated faces $\widehat G$ for the same $G$. This follows by adding the two slab inequalities to the facet inequalities of $C$; any proper face not contained in an end hyperplane is obtained from original facet equalities. A face contained in an end hyperplane is a face of that end section. Thus $\widehat C$ has exactly the face incidences of the product prism $C_a\times[a,b]$, with end faces distinguished. These incidences agree on intersections of cells of $\mathcal K$.

Construct the maps by induction over these common face incidences. On each bottom face use the identity. On the top faces choose compatible PL maps from their corresponding bottom faces as follows: match vertices using the face correspondence, and extend over each higher-dimensional face by coning its already defined boundary map from an interior point to an interior point. Both faces are convex, so the cones cover them with disjoint relative interiors, proving bijectivity and a PL inverse. For every remaining, vertical face pair choose interior points at height $(a+b)/2$ on both sides; such points exist by step 1.1. The height on the source prism is its second coordinate. Once the boundary map is constructed, triangulate the boundary compatibly and extend over that face by coning between these two interior points. The same convex-cone argument proves that this is a PL homeomorphism on the face. It preserves height: its boundary map already does, its two cone points have the same height, and height is affine on each cone simplex. This induction includes the full truncated cells. Shared faces have only one previously prescribed map, so all maps agree on intersections. Only finitely many cells occur.

Paste the maps to obtain $H$. A point in the relative interior of a source prism cell maps to the relative interior of its corresponding target cell, so the pasted map is a bijection. The cellwise inverses agree on intersections and paste to its inverse. Both are PL on finite compatible subdivisions furnished by [F1], hence continuous. The bottom restriction and height identity follow from step 3.1. A union of original cells is a union of the corresponding prism cells, giving the compatibility assertion. If $P_a$ is empty there is no cell meeting the slab by step 1.1, so both sides are empty. All selections involved finite sets of cells and interior points, and require no countable or arbitrary-index choice.

derivations.claim: Its intersection with $z=0$ consists of two distinct rays. Choose a homogeneous PL homeomorphism $g:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ taking them to the positive and negative $x$-axis. Explicitly, insert finitely many further rays to divide both plane sectors between the two marked rays into sectors of angle less than $\pi$, do the same for the two target half-planes with corresponding numbers of sectors, and match their cyclically ordered ray generators. Extend linearly on each sector. Each sector map is a linear bijection onto its corresponding convex sector; these maps and their linear inverses agree on rays and paste to inverse PL homeomorphisms. Extend to three-space by $G(u,z)=(g(u),z)$. Replace $S$ temporarily by $G(S)$. Both its horizontal zero rays are now the $x$-axis rays, and $G$ preserves height.

The sections $L_+=S\cap\{z=1\}$ and $L_-=\{u:(u,-1)\in S\}$ are each simple proper polygonal lines with finitely many bends and exactly two unbounded rays, one tending to each end of the $x$-direction. To see this, radial projection from each open link arc to its level $z=1$ or $z=-1$ is a homeomorphism. A cone triangle meets that level in a segment, ray or empty set; the finitely many triangles therefore give a polygonal line. Near either endpoint of the link arc its last linear cone sector meets the level in a ray parallel to the corresponding horizontal zero ray. These are its only ends; the projection is proper because any compact part of the level has directions bounded away from $z=0$. The same statements remain valid after step 1.1: a ray eventually lies in one sector of the finite homogeneous fan, and its image is a ray parallel to the image of its limiting direction. Thus both lines have horizontal terminal rays directed to opposite ends.

We give an explicit finite PL plane homeomorphism $f$ straightening any such line $L$, with bounded displacement. Take a rectangle $R=[-r,r]\times[-h,h]$ whose interior contains all bends of $L$ and whose two vertical sides meet its horizontal terminal rays once each; enlarge $r,h$ so all finite segments lie in its interior and these are the only boundary intersections. The arc $L\cap R$ divides $R$ into two polygonal disks. Indeed each union of that arc with one of the two boundary arcs between its endpoints is a simple polygon. By the planar separation and disk assertion of [F1], their bounded disks occupy precisely the two sides inside $R$: near the top and bottom edges they occupy the respective sides, their interiors are disjoint by crossing parity, and every point of $R\setminus L$ connects within its polygonal component to one of those sides. Choose on $\partial R$ an order-preserving PL map fixing both horizontal sides and all corners and taking the two line endpoints to $(-r,0)$ and $(r,0)$. Choose any order-preserving PL parameter of the finite line arc onto the horizontal diameter. On each of the two disks these prescriptions form a boundary homeomorphism onto the corresponding upper or lower half-rectangle. Extend them by [F1]. Their maps agree on the line arc, so they give a PL homeomorphism $f_R:R\to R$ taking that arc to the diameter.

Write the two vertical boundary maps of $f_R$ as $(-r,y)\mapsto(-r,\gamma_-(y))$ and $(r,y)\mapsto(r,\gamma_+(y))$. Both $\gamma_\pm$ are increasing PL homeomorphisms of $[-h,h]$, fix its endpoints, and send the respective terminal-ray height to zero. Outside $R$ extend $f_R$ on the two half-strips by $f(x,y)=(x,\gamma_+(y))$ for $x\ge r$ and $|y|\le h$, and by the corresponding formula with $\gamma_-$ for $x\le-r$. Use the identity for $|y|\ge h$. These formulas agree along every seam. Their inverses have the same form with $\gamma_\pm^{-1}$, so the extension is a PL plane homeomorphism. Its cells consist of finitely many bounded triangles, half-strips and exterior half-planes, all with compatible finite polyhedral subdivisions; their intersections with a bounded box admit finite simplicial subdivisions by [F2]. It sends the entire $L$ to the $x$-axis. Moreover $f(u)-u$ is bounded: on $R$ this follows from compactness, on the half-strips only the second coordinate changes by at most $2h$, and elsewhere it is zero. Its inverse also has bounded displacement, since $f^{-1}(v)-v=u-f(u)$ for $v=f(u)$. Apply this construction independently to $L_+$ and $L_-$, producing $f_+$ and $f_-$.

For $z>0$ set $T(u,z)=(z f_+(u/z),z)$. For $z<0$ put $s=-z>0$ and set $T(u,z)=(s f_-(u/s),z)$. Set $T(u,0)=(u,0)$. These formulas define a finite PL homeomorphism. To check the PL assertion, on a plane cell where $f_\pm(v)=Av+b$ its homogenization is $(u,z)\mapsto(Au+zb,z)$ above zero, or $(u,z)\mapsto(Au-zb,z)$ below zero. The homogenized cells are polyhedral cones: an inequality $av\le c$ becomes $au\le cz$ above zero or $au\le-cz$ below zero. There are finitely many such cones. Their intersections with each bounded cube have compatible finite simplicial subdivisions by [F2]; subdividing successive integer cube shells compatibly, always coning from the barycenter of the vertices of each clipped cell, gives the usual locally finite PL interpretation without any countable choice of centers. Bounded displacement implies that their linear formulas match the identity on the zero plane: $\|z f_+(u/z)-u\|\le M_+z$ and $\|s f_-(u/s)-u\|\le M_-s$. Hence the formulas extend continuously and agree there. Homogenizing the inverse maps in the same way supplies an inverse with identical continuity and PL properties. In particular $T$ preserves height and fixes the zero plane pointwise.

Every positive-height point of the cone $S$ is uniquely $(zv,z)$ with $v\in L_+$, and every negative-height point is uniquely $(sv,-s)$ with $v\in L_-$. By step 4.1 their images under $T$ are exactly the positive and negative parts of the vertical plane $y=0$. Its zero-height part is already the full $x$-axis. Therefore $H=T\circ G$, with $G$ from step 1.1 and $T$ applied to the transformed cone, has all the stated properties. For the local consequence take a sufficiently small star at the surface vertex: its finitely many incident triangles agree there with their full cones. Restrict $H$ to a smaller neighborhood of the origin; it gives the required height-preserving local straightening. All fans, polygonal disk extensions, rectangles and affine cells used finite data, so no countable or arbitrary-index choice is needed.

derivations.claim: First consider a compact finite polyhedron $Y$ with a PL function $q:Y\to[0,M]$, zero set $X$, and a PL collar $c:X\times[0,1]\to Y$ of $X$. Its image contains an open neighborhood $U$ of $X$. The compact complement $Y\setminus U$ has strictly positive minimum $q$ when nonempty. Thus, for sufficiently small positive $\eta$, the whole set $q^{-1}([0,\eta])$ lies in the collar image. On the collar domain let $r(x,s)=s$ and $k(x,s)=q(c(x,s))$. Both are PL, nonnegative, and vanish precisely on $X\times\{0\}$: injectivity of $c$ precludes any other collar point from mapping to the zero set. Choose a finite triangulation of the domain on which $c,r,k$ are linear, with the bottom a subcomplex, by [F2]. Corresponding source and image simplices of $c$ consequently have exactly the same zero vertices, all their other vertices having strictly positive $r$ and $q$ values. Choose $0<\delta<\eta$ smaller than all these finitely many positive values.

Cut each source simplex by $r\le\delta$ and its corresponding image simplex by $q\le\delta$. Only simplices with at least one zero vertex occur. On a mixed simplex the truncated polytope has its original zero face, its top section at $\delta$, and the truncated faces of the original simplex. Its vertices are the zero vertices and the intersections of zero-positive edges with the top section. In particular its face incidences depend only on which original vertices are zero, not on the strictly positive values at the remaining vertices. This assertion follows directly from the simplex inequalities $\lambda_i\ge0$, $\sum\lambda_i=1$ and the cut $\sum q_i\lambda_i\le\delta$: the cut meets exactly the edges from zero vertices to positive vertices and no edge joining positive vertices. The corresponding truncated source and target cells therefore have identical face posets, compatible on common faces. Their zero faces are identified pointwise by $c(x,0)=x$.

Construct compatible PL homeomorphisms of these truncated cells, preserving $r$ as target height $q$. On zero faces use the identity. On top faces, match the corresponding vertices and extend inductively over their faces by coning from relative interior points; all these points have height $\delta$, so these maps preserve height. Any remaining face spans heights zero to $\delta$ and has a relative interior point at height $\delta/2$ on both sides: its section at that level meets its relative interior by convexity. Having already defined its boundary map, triangulate the boundary compatibly and cone that map between those two points. Convexity makes each extension bijective with PL inverse. Height is preserved on every cone simplex because it is affine, agrees on the boundary, and has equal values at the two cone points. Induction over faces gives a PL homeomorphism from the entire source truncation $X\times[0,\delta]$ onto the target truncation $q^{-1}([0,\delta])$, fixed on the bottom and with $q$ equal to the parameter. The target equality uses the neighborhood inclusion from step 1.1. Thus every collar satisfying the stated positivity has an exact short height-product replacement, rather than only an abstract collar parameter.

Apply this construction to each $t<b$, with $Y=P_{\ge t}$ and $q=h-t$. The fiber $X_t$ is a compact subpolyhedron by [F2], and [F1] supplies its collar in $Y$. Hence a whole short upper slab has a height-product parameter based on $X_t$. For $t>a$ apply it to $Y=P_{\le t}$ and $q=t-h$ for a lower slab. Paste the two parameters at their common identity bottom fiber, reversing the lower parameter. This gives a PL height-product parameter $\Phi_t:X_t\times J_t\to h^{-1}(J_t)$ on a relative open interval $J_t$ about $t$ in $[a,b]$, after restricting the closed short parameters slightly if necessary. At endpoints use just the one-sided parameter. All fibers are nonempty by surjectivity.

The intervals $J_t$ cover $[a,b]$. Compactness gives a finite subcover and a finite subdivision $a=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=b$ such that each closed interval $[t_{i-1},t_i]$ is contained in one $J_{s_i}$. For completeness, such a subdivision can be selected without an infinite sequence of choices: a finite open interval cover of a compact real interval has a positive Lebesgue number, as follows by taking, at each point, an interval contained in one cover member, then a finite subcover by intervals of half that radius and the minimum of their finitely many half-radii. Any sufficiently fine equal subdivision works. Restrict $\Phi_{s_i}$ to the corresponding closed subinterval. Its inverse at height $t_{i-1}$ identifies that initial fiber with $X_{s_i}$. Reparametrize this restricted product by that identification to obtain $\Psi_i:X_{t_{i-1}}\times[t_{i-1},t_i]\to h^{-1}([t_{i-1},t_i])$ with $\Psi_i(y,t_{i-1})=y$.

Define $H$ inductively. On the first band put $H(x,t)=\Psi_1(x,t)$. On the $i$th band put $H(x,t)=\Psi_i(H(x,t_{i-1}),t)$. These formulas agree at the joining fibers, are PL on finite compatible subdivisions, and preserve height. On every fiber the map is a composition of PL homeomorphisms; the inverse formulas likewise paste on the bands. Therefore $H$ is a PL homeomorphism onto $P$ with the claimed initial restriction. A local height-product chart supplies exactly the local collar charts used in step 4.1. Every cover, subdivision, cell extension and selection in this proof is finite; no countable or arbitrary-index choice was used.

Here a parametrized PL ball means a finite polyhedron supplied with a piecewise linear homeomorphism, with piecewise linear inverse, to a convex polyhedral ball of the stated dimension. All subpolyhedra and maps in the following assertions are finite.

(a) Let $B_1,B_2$ be parametrized PL three-balls and $D_i\subset\partial B_i$ parametrized PL two-disks. Every PL homeomorphism $f:D_1\to D_2$ extends to a PL homeomorphism $B_1\to B_2$.

(b) The space obtained by gluing two parametrized PL three-balls along parametrized PL two-disks in their boundaries, by a specified PL homeomorphism, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

(c) Let $B$ and $A\subset B$ be parametrized PL three-balls, with $A\ne B$. Suppose $A\cap\partial B=\partial A\cap\partial B=D$ is a parametrized PL two-disk and $A\setminus D\subset\operatorname{Int}B$. Impose the following standard boundary-window condition at $C=\partial D$: every point of $C$ has a PL coordinate neighborhood in which
$$B=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0\},\qquad A=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0,\ v\le0\},\qquad D=\{w=0,\ v\le0\}.$$
The equalities are understood after intersection with the coordinate neighborhood, and $C$ corresponds to $v=w=0$. Then $Q=\overline{B\setminus A}$, with closure in $B$, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

No assertion about a sphere in an arbitrary PL three-manifold is assumed. In (c) the closure of the set difference is essential: $B\setminus\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb R^3}A$ would retain the interior of the contact disk as an extra sheet. These statements introduce no choice hypothesis.

In this statement, finite PL means affine on finitely many convex polyhedral pieces, which may be unbounded; on every bounded subpolyhedron compatible finite simplicial subdivisions give the usual PL interpretation. Let $S\subset\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R$ be a finite polyhedral cone with vertex $0$ whose intersection with a small centered polyhedral sphere is a simple polygonal circle. Write $z$ for the last coordinate. Suppose this circle meets $z=0$ in exactly two points, each a crossing from $z>0$ to $z<0$, and neither lies on a segment contained in $z=0$. Equivalently, the positive and negative parts of the circle are each one open arc and its zero set is their two endpoints. Then there is a finite piecewise linear homeomorphism $H:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, with piecewise linear inverse, such that
$$z(H(x,y,z))=z,\qquad H(S)=\{(x,0,z):x,z\in\mathbb R\}.$$
It fixes the origin. Its restriction to $z=0$ is a homogeneous PL plane homeomorphism sending the two rays of $S\cap\{z=0\}$ to the two rays of the $x$-axis.

Consequently a polyhedral surface in linear three-space at a vertex having this regular height-link condition has a local PL straightening preserving its affine height. This is a local regular-vertex result, not a straightening of arbitrary PL two-spheres. No choice hypothesis is introduced.

Let $P$ be a compact finite polyhedron and $h:P\to[a,b]$ a surjective PL function, where $a<b$. Write $X_t=h^{-1}(t)$, $P_{\ge t}=h^{-1}([t,b])$ and $P_{\le t}=h^{-1}([a,t])$. Suppose, for every $t<b$, $X_t$ is locally PL collared in $P_{\ge t}$ and, for every $t>a$, it is locally PL collared in $P_{\le t}$. Local collars here have open half-product images, including at boundary points of the fiber. Then there is a PL homeomorphism with PL inverse
$$H:X_a\times[a,b]\longrightarrow P,\qquad H(x,a)=x,\qquad h(H(x,t))=t.$$
The construction is finite and introduces no choice hypothesis. In particular this conclusion holds when each point has a local PL height-product chart, with the appropriate one-sided chart at the end levels.

derivations.claim: We will use the following finite two-dimensional link construction. A simple polygonal circle $C$ in a standard PL two-sphere bounds two parametrized PL disks. To verify it, replace the sphere by a tetrahedral boundary using its supplied standard parameter and choose a tetrahedral vertex $q$ off $C$. If necessary move a point off $C$ to that vertex by finitely many small polygonal chart point pushes, each obtained by moving the center of a triangle fan in a convex polygon and fixing its boundary. Truncate a sufficiently small cone at $q$ disjoint from $C$. The remainder of the tetrahedral boundary has a finite planar disk parameter: its opposite face maps to a smaller concentric planar triangle, and its three quadrilateral strips to the surrounding triangular annulus, by the disk boundary extension in [F1]. The image of $C$ is a simple polygon inside this triangle. Its inner disk is supplied by [F1]. The region between it and the outer triangle is a PL annulus: cut along a thin strip about a polygonal joining arc, parametrize the resulting polygonal disk by [F1], then restore the strip. Filling the annulus's outer end with the removed cone at $q$ gives the second disk. The same disk boundary-extension result makes their common circle parameters agree. Consequently a cone on either link disk is a half-ball, and coning the two compatible disk parameters gives the standard local pair of a plane and its two half-spaces. This construction applies to the link circle at every point of $S$, including points made vertices by subdivision.

Construct a compact finite polyhedral region with boundary $S$ without assuming a three-dimensional separation theorem. Choose a point $p$ off the finitely many triangle planes and cone each triangle $\tau$ of $S$ to $p$, obtaining finitely many nondegenerate tetrahedra. Regard their sum with coefficients in $\mathbb F_2$. Its boundary is exactly the triangle sum of $S$: the cone on each sphere edge occurs twice and cancels. Subdivide the union of these tetrahedra by their finitely many face planes and triangulate compatibly by [F2]. Give each full-dimensional cell the parity of the number of tetrahedra containing its interior, and let $Q$ be the union of the closures of odd cells. It is a compact finite polyhedron. At a generic point of a subdivision face not in $S$, the two adjacent parity coefficients agree by the preceding boundary cancellation; at a face in $S$ they differ by one. Thus parity extends as a locally constant function on $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$ and changes across $S$. To justify extension at subdivision edges or vertices off $S$, join nearby full-dimensional cells by a small polygonal path missing the codimension-two skeleton; each crossed face is outside $S$ and preserves parity. At a point of $S$, use the two half-ball charts of step 1.1; on each side the same small-path argument makes parity constant, and a transverse face crossing shows the two values differ. Therefore $\partial Q=S$ and $Q$ has a local PL half-ball chart along $S$ and an ordinary interior chart elsewhere.

Both sides of $S$ are connected. The local $Q$ side along $S$ belongs to a single component of $\operatorname{Int}Q$: each surface chart has a connected half-ball side, and paths in the connected sphere propagate that component from one chart to the next. Any additional component would have a nonempty boundary in $S$, since an open nonempty bounded component cannot be closed in $\mathbb R^3$; a boundary point would contradict the chart description just given. The same reasoning applies to $\mathbb R^3\setminus Q$: all its local sides along $S$ belong to one component, and any component has a boundary point in $S$ unless it is both open and closed in $\mathbb R^3$. Hence it is connected; it contains the complement of a large box and is unbounded. These arguments use only elementary polygonal path connectedness of open subsets and connectedness of Euclidean space; a nonempty bounded open component has a boundary point by intersecting a segment from one of its points to a point outside its closure. Thus $Q$ is precisely the closure of the bounded side. Moreover $h$ achieves its minimum and maximum on $Q$ at $S$: an interior extremum of a nonconstant affine coordinate is impossible. They are consequently $h(v_-)$ and $h(v_+)$.

At the minimum vertex $v_-$, the whole surface link lies strictly above its horizontal plane. The link disk on the $Q$ side supplied by step 1.1 also lies strictly above that plane. Indeed the complementary link component contains every lower direction, which cannot belong to $Q$ by step 3.1; hence the $Q$ link is the other disk, disjoint from the closed lower hemisphere. Choose $\alpha>h(v_-)$ sufficiently close to the minimum that $Q\cap\{h\le\alpha\}$ lies within the conical star of this vertex. Such a choice exists by compactness of the complement of any smaller vertex neighborhood, whose minimum height is strictly larger. In that star the set is exactly the cone from $v_-$ to its planar section $D_-=Q\cap\{h=\alpha\}$. This section is a parametrized polygonal disk: radial projection of the upper link disk to the section plane is a homeomorphism, and each cone face cuts it in a finite straight segment. Its boundary is a simple polygon, its interior is its bounded side, and [F1] supplies a finite PL disk parameter. Coning that parameter from $v_-$ gives a PL parameter of the cap as a three-ball. Apply the reversed-height argument at $v_+$ to obtain $\beta< h(v_+)$ with a parametrized upper cap and disk section $D_+$. Take the caps small enough that $\alpha<\beta$ and neither end level contains a sphere vertex.

Every point of the middle band $P=Q\cap\{\alpha\le h\le\beta\}$ has a local PL height-product chart, with a one-sided chart at the two end levels.
