derivations.claim: Choose a saddle plane $h=a$ with critical vertex $q$. The section is a finite graph with every point of degree two except $q$, whose degree is $2r_q$. Following each edge from $q$ until it first returns to $q$ decomposes its nonregular component into simple loops; distinct loops meet only at $q$. Other components are simple circles. A finite collection of such planar loops has an innermost simple loop $C$ bounding a polygonal disk $D$ with $\operatorname{Int}D\cap S=\varnothing$: choose an innermost bounded complementary face inside a loop, and if its boundary passes $q$, follow its simple loop boundary; the only possible common vertex is $q$. The circle $C$ cuts $S$ into two parametrized PL disks $E_1,E_2$. To check the finite PL parameter assertion, transfer to the supplied standard sphere, choose a tetrahedral vertex off the transferred circle by polygonal chart point pushes, and truncate a small cone disjoint from it. The remaining sphere has a planar triangular disk parameter by mapping its opposite face and three strips to concentric triangles. Apply [F1] to the circle there; the other disk is the surrounding annulus capped by the removed cone, parametrized by cutting a joining strip and using [F1]. Thus $\Sigma_i=E_i\cup D$ are finite PL spheres, with their flat caps explicitly parametrized.

First suppose $q\notin C$. In each $E_i$ a sufficiently narrow collar of $C$ lies entirely on one side of $h=a$, since $C$ has no critical point and the collar's open connected side has constant height sign. Write $t=\pm(h-a)\ge0$ with that sign. For small $0<t\le\epsilon$, the collar meets its level plane in one polygonal circle $C_t$ approaching $C$. Its bounded planar disk $D_t$ varies in a finite polyhedral layer $Z$ with bottom $D$ and side that collar: subdivide by the finitely many incident triangle planes and use planar crossing parity to select the bounded disk cells. Taking $\epsilon$ small keeps every other surface part outside $Z$. Away from $C$ this follows from the positive separation of compact nonincident pieces and $\operatorname{Int}D\cap S=\varnothing$; along $C$ it follows from the ordinary two-face regular height charts. The layer is a PL manifold with boundary: interior cells have ball charts, side points have half-ball charts, and its bottom rim has quadrant charts from the same planar fans. Its level fibers have local collars at both sides, including its bottom and top. Thus [F3] supplies a height-product disk parameter on all of $Z$. Apply [F4] to replace $D$ and the collar by a cap with one extremum and otherwise regular height. The rest of $E_i$ meets $Z$ only in its top circle. The ball-transfer conclusion of [F4] is therefore applicable. This supplies the required cap replacement for $\Sigma_i$ in the nonpointed case.

Now suppose $q\in C$. For each $i$, the open boundary arc $C\setminus\{q\}$ has a one-sided collar in $E_i$ of constant height sign. Orient $t=\pm(h-a)$ with this sign. Choose one positive ray in each of its two incident face sectors at $q$, very close to the corresponding zero ray of $C$, and call them $\rho_1,\rho_2$. For small $0<t\le\epsilon$, the part of the collar between these rays is one embedded polygonal arc $l_t$ joining $t\rho_1$ to $t\rho_2$; choose ray generators of height one. This follows by tracing the level segments in the finitely many incident triangles along $C\setminus\{q\}$; none of their other vertices has height between zero and $\epsilon$. The two terminal sectors are linear cones. The planar disk $D$ has an empty angular sector at $q$: its link arc lies in the horizontal circle and meets no other surface direction except its endpoints, since its interior is disjoint from the section graph. Just inside the chosen positive side of this arc choose a finite polygonal joining arc at level $\epsilon$ from $\epsilon\rho_1$ to $\epsilon\rho_2$, disjoint from $S$ except at its ends. Such an arc is obtained by following that empty link sector and projecting radially to the positive level; its compact interior stays in the adjacent open complementary sector. Call this arc $g_\epsilon$ and put $g_t=(t/\epsilon)g_\epsilon$. Then $l_t\cup g_t$ is a simple polygon. Its bounded disk $D_t$ contains no other surface piece: away from $q$ use finite positive separations as in step 2.1; in the small conical neighborhood of $q$, the chosen joining arc cuts off exactly the sector adjacent to the empty disk, excluding the remaining link branches. Shrink $\epsilon$ once for these finitely many requirements.

Let $Z$ be the layer of these disks for $0<t\le\epsilon$, with bottom $D$. It is a compact finite polyhedron: its boundary consists of the bottom disk, the finite surface strip $L=\bigcup l_t$, the cone $G=\bigcup g_t=q*g_\epsilon$, and the top disk $T=D_\epsilon$; a common plane arrangement with planar parity selects its finitely many solid cells. It is a PL manifold with boundary, also at $q$. The link there has boundary made of the bottom disk arc, two positive surface-sector arcs and the closing arc of $G$, forming one simple polygonal circle on the standard link sphere. The disk on its positive side gives its half-ball chart. The disk assertion follows by the finite tetrahedral planar chart and [F1] as in step 1.1; coning gives the chart. The bottom arc is an ordinary boundary interval of that link disk, so $D$ is locally collared even at $q$. Everywhere at positive height, the side arcs and their endpoints give the ordinary half-space or quadrant height charts; there are no other vertices of the surface in the layer. Therefore [F3] gives a height-product parameter $D\times[0,\epsilon]\to Z$. In particular $Z$ is a supplied parametrized PL ball. The old cap part $F=D\cup L$ is a disk with boundary $l_\epsilon\cup\rho_1[0,\epsilon]\cup\rho_2[0,\epsilon]$. Splitting its strip corner $q$ into its two boundary occurrences makes $L$ a finite PL disk with bottom the interval obtained by cutting $C$ at $q$, top $l_\epsilon$ and two monotone sides $\rho_1,\rho_2$. Its bottom and positive fibers have local one-sided collars, so [F3] also supplies a height-product interval parameter for this normalized strip. Restoring the two occurrences gives the actual strip in $\partial Z$.

Supply the convex pointed boundary model required by [F5], rather than assuming it. Let $D_0=[0,2]^2\times\{0\}$ with $q_0=(0,0,0)$, and take the convex hull with the top triangle having vertices $(-1,1,\epsilon),(1,-1,\epsilon),(1,1,\epsilon)$. Its face in $x+y=0$ is the triangle $G_0$ from $q_0$ to the first two top vertices, meeting $D_0$ only at $q_0$. The remaining side strip, normalized by splitting $q_0$, has a height-product interval parameter by the same [F3] argument, or directly from its convex faces. Map $D$ to $D_0$, taking $q$ to $q_0$, by [F1]. Match the two normalized strip parameters by their induced bottom interval map; this is height-preserving and matches the two side rays at every height. Map the cone $G$ to $G_0$ by coning its top arc map linearly from $q$ to $q_0$; choose its endpoints to match the strip maps. On the top disk extend the already prescribed boundary map by [F1]. These four maps paste to a finite PL boundary homeomorphism preserving height on $D,L,G,T$. All hypotheses of [F5] are now supplied. Its supporting-plane cut replaces a subdisk of $F$ containing $D$ by a pointed cap meeting $t=0$ only at $q$, introducing no positive-height saddle. The old sphere meets the cut ball only in that subdisk, by step 3.1, so [F5]'s ball transfer applies. The replacement is confined to an arbitrarily short positive height range. On the critical plane it deletes precisely the chosen loop $C$; all other branches at $q$ are outside the layer and remain unchanged.

Perform the respective replacements on both $\Sigma_i$, in a height range containing no other original saddle height, obtaining $S'_i$. In step 2.1 only a new extremum was inserted. In step 5.1 all new positive-height points are regular, and at height $a$ exactly the selected loop has disappeared. Every other original critical-plane loop belongs to one of the two cut disks and is unchanged. If the remaining vertex at height $a$ becomes regular or an extremum in either sphere, that plane no longer contributes to its complexity, which can only decrease the count further. Thus the total contribution at this height is at most the former contribution minus one; at other saddle heights the contributions partition the original ones. Restore generic affine heights by arbitrarily small direction perturbations and compatible subdivisions. This does not add saddles: each new nonextremal vertex has a link circle with exactly two transverse zero crossings, a condition stable under a small perturbation on its finite link edges; the cap extremum has all incident directions of one sign. The other critical link signs and the order of their heights are preserved by choosing the perturbation below the finitely many nonzero sign and height gaps. There are no horizontal surface faces left in the replaced caps. The section graph incidence at each unchanged critical vertex is determined by these signs, so its loop count is preserved. This proves the stated complexity inequality. Finally, supplied balls for $S'_i$ transfer by steps 2.1 or 5.1 to supplied balls for $\Sigma_i$. Apply [F6] to the three disks $E_1,E_2,D$ to obtain the ball bounded by $S$. All constructions and exclusions were finite, so no choice principle was introduced.

citations.quote: Let $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a finite linearly embedded triangulated two-sphere and $h$ an affine height function taking distinct values on its vertices. Assume there is exactly one minimum vertex $v_-$, exactly one maximum vertex $v_+$, and every other vertex has the following regular height link: its small centered polyhedral link circle meets the horizontal plane through that vertex in exactly two crossing points, with its positive and negative parts each one open arc. Then $S$ is the boundary of a compact finite polyhedron $Q\subset\mathbb R^3$ admitting a finite PL homeomorphism, with PL inverse, to a convex three-ball. The set $Q$ is the closure of the bounded side of $S$, and the other side is connected and unbounded. No choice hypothesis or general three-dimensional Schoenflies theorem is assumed.

Let $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a supplied finite PL embedding of the standard PL two-sphere. Choose an affine height $h$ distinct on the vertices of a linear triangulation of $S$. At a vertex $v$ with both lower and upper incident directions, let $r_v$ be the number of positive arcs of its small link circle; it is also the number of negative arcs. Call $v$ a saddle when $r_v\ge2$. Its horizontal section consists of $r_v$ simple loops meeting only at $v$, together with finitely many disjoint regular circles. Let $n(S,h)$ be the sum of the numbers of all these loops, including the regular circles, over the distinct saddle heights.

If $n(S,h)>0$, there are two supplied finite PL embedded two-spheres $S'_1,S'_2$, with generic affine heights $h_1,h_2$, for which
$$n(S'_1,h_1)+n(S'_2,h_2)\le n(S,h)-1.$$
Moreover supplied parametrized PL balls bounded by $S'_1,S'_2$ give, by explicit finite PL constructions, a parametrized PL ball bounded by $S$. No general three-dimensional Schoenflies theorem or choice hypothesis is used.

Here a parametrized PL ball means a finite polyhedron supplied with a piecewise linear homeomorphism, with piecewise linear inverse, to a convex polyhedral ball of the stated dimension. All subpolyhedra and maps in the following assertions are finite.

(a) Let $B_1,B_2$ be parametrized PL three-balls and $D_i\subset\partial B_i$ parametrized PL two-disks. Every PL homeomorphism $f:D_1\to D_2$ extends to a PL homeomorphism $B_1\to B_2$.

(b) The space obtained by gluing two parametrized PL three-balls along parametrized PL two-disks in their boundaries, by a specified PL homeomorphism, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

(c) Let $B$ and $A\subset B$ be parametrized PL three-balls, with $A\ne B$. Suppose $A\cap\partial B=\partial A\cap\partial B=D$ is a parametrized PL two-disk and $A\setminus D\subset\operatorname{Int}B$. Impose the following standard boundary-window condition at $C=\partial D$: every point of $C$ has a PL coordinate neighborhood in which
$$B=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0\},\qquad A=\{(u,v,w):w\ge0,\ v\le0\},\qquad D=\{w=0,\ v\le0\}.$$
The equalities are understood after intersection with the coordinate neighborhood, and $C$ corresponds to $v=w=0$. Then $Q=\overline{B\setminus A}$, with closure in $B$, is a parametrized PL three-ball.

No assertion about a sphere in an arbitrary PL three-manifold is assumed. In (c) the closure of the set difference is essential: $B\setminus\operatorname{Int}_{\mathbb R^3}A$ would retain the interior of the contact disk as an extra sheet. These statements introduce no choice hypothesis.

Every finite convex cell complex has a compatible finite simplicial triangulation. Choose one relative interior point in each nonempty cell; triangulate the boundary in increasing dimension and cone from that point. This construction agrees on every common face and preserves each cell as a subpolyhedron.

derivations.claim: Compute the finite height index sum. Assign each simplex of the surface triangulation to its highest vertex. The contribution at a vertex $v$ to the alternating vertex-edge-triangle count is $1-\chi(L_v^-)$, where $L_v^-$ is its lower link: an assigned incident edge contributes minus one for each lower link vertex and an assigned incident triangle contributes plus one for each lower link edge. If all directions are above $v$, the lower link is empty and the contribution is one. If all are below, it is the whole link circle, whose Euler characteristic is zero, again giving one. Otherwise it is a disjoint union of $r_v$ intervals, giving contribution $1-r_v$. These interval components are counted by the positive and negative link arcs of [F2]. Summing over vertices gives $$m+M-\sum_{v\text{ saddle}}(r_v-1)=2,$$ where $m,M$ are the numbers of minimum and maximum vertices. The right side is the Euler count of the standard sphere. It can be checked in the boundary of a tetrahedron and is unchanged by finite common subdivisions: subdividing an edge or coning a subdivided triangle boundary preserves the alternating count, by the interval and disk face counts. The supplied finite PL sphere parameter gives such common subdivisions with the tetrahedral boundary.

If $n=0$, there are no saddles, since a saddle section contains at least its two loops and contributes positively to $n$. Step 1.1 gives $m+M=2$. Both are at least one because the finite nonconstant height has a minimum and maximum, so $m=M=1$. Every other vertex has $r_v=1$, precisely the regular height-link condition. Apply [F1] to obtain a finite PL ball parameter. For general $n$ use strong induction: when $n>0$, [F2] gives two embedded parametrized PL spheres with nonnegative complexities $n_1,n_2$ satisfying $n_1+n_2\le n-1$. Hence each is smaller than $n$, so the induction hypothesis supplies their PL balls. The explicit transfer and reassembly operations of [F2] supply the ball bounded by $S$. This is a finite induction terminating at the zero case, not a citation to a general Schoenflies theorem.

The complement of this parametrized ball has a connected unbounded exterior. A finite compatible link subdivision gives local plane/half-space charts at its boundary: the boundary link circle splits the standard two-sphere link into two parametrized disks by the polygonal planar chart construction. Its interior has ball charts transported by its supplied ball parameter. Along the connected boundary, exterior half-ball charts chain into one complement component. Every other complement component would have a boundary point on that boundary, contradicting these charts; an open component with no boundary in connected Euclidean space would be all of Euclidean space. The exterior contains the complement of a large box and is therefore unbounded. The bounded component is the connected ball interior. This proves all complementary-component assertions in $\mathbb R^3$.

We describe the standard ambient charts needed to pass to $S^3$ without a manifold triangulation theorem. Realize standard PL $S^3$ as the boundary of a four-simplex. A point off the embedded sphere can be carried to a fixed vertex by finitely many PL point pushes in linear ball charts along a polygonal path: triangulate a small convex ball by coning its boundary from the current point and move that cone point to a sufficiently close next point, fixing the boundary. The punctured four-simplex boundary has an explicit locally finite PL chart to $\mathbb R^3$: map the opposite three-face to a convex tetrahedron, and successive truncated conical shells toward the deleted vertex to successive shells between tetrahedra of radii $2^j$. Their matching convex cell decompositions have compatible face-cone maps by [F4]. On every compact subset only finitely many shells occur. The shell cells and cone points can be determined from their vertices and barycenters, so this description requires no countable choice. Thus the given compact sphere becomes a finite polyhedral sphere in $\mathbb R^3$. Step 2.1 supplies one complementary PL ball in $S^3$.

Choose a point in that ball's interior and apply the same explicit punctured standard-sphere chart at this new point. The previously unbounded complementary side is now bounded: the omitted point lies on the other side, and a neighborhood of that point is disjoint from this side's compact closure. Step 2.1 in this chart supplies its PL ball parameter. The complementary-side identifications follow from step 3.1 applied in the charts, so these are exactly the two closed complementary balls of the original sphere. Their supplied boundary maps differ by a PL sphere homeomorphism. Extend that homeomorphism over one convex model by coning a compatible boundary triangulation from its interior point; this is the same finite extension used in [F3]. Adjusting that ball parameter makes the two boundary parameters agree. Paste them to obtain a PL homeomorphism from $S^3$ to the double of a convex three-ball, taking the embedded sphere to the common boundary. Both domains are compact finite polyhedra, so the pasted parameters and inverses have finite compatible subdivisions. All selections, chart restrictions, index computations, cap reductions and gluings used finite data. No choice principle is needed, and no arbitrary topological ambient manifold has been given a PL structure in this argument.
